151: API Reference
152: Ask about this section
153: Copy for LLM
154: View as Markdown
155: The Stripe API is organized around REST. Our API has predictable resource-oriented URLs, accepts form-encoded request bodies, returns JSON-encoded responses, and uses standard HTTP response codes, authentication, and verbs.
156: You can use the Stripe API in sandboxes without affecting your live data or interacting with banking networks. The API key that you use to authenticate the request determines whether the request runs in live mode or in a sandbox. Sandboxes support all v2 APIs. Test mode sandboxes support some v2 APIs.
157: The Stripe API doesn’t support bulk updates. You can work on only one object per request.
158: The Stripe API differs for every account as we release new versions and tailor functionality. Log in to see docs with your test key and data.
159: Was this section helpful?YesNo
160: Just getting started?
161: Check out our development quickstart guide.
162: Not a developer?
163: Use Stripe’s no-code options or apps from our partners to get started with Stripe and to do more with your Stripe account—no code required.
164: Base URL
165: https://api.stripe.com
166: Client Libraries
167: Ruby
168: Python
169: PHP
170: Java
171: Node.js
172: Go
173: .NET
174: By default, the Stripe API Docs demonstrate using curl to interact with the API over HTTP. Select one of our official client libraries to see examples in code.
175: Authentication
176: Ask about this section
177: Copy for LLM
178: View as Markdown
179: The Stripe API uses API keys to authenticate requests. You can view and manage your API keys in the Stripe Dashboard.
180: Test mode secret keys start with sk_test_ and have unrestricted access to their sandboxes. In live mode, you configure a restricted API key (starts with rk_live_) with specific API permissions. Using a restricted API key with only a subset of API permissions limits the damage a bad actor could cause if they obtained the key. In both test mode and live mode, you can create as many restricted API keys as you need for different use cases or components of your application. We also create a live mode secret key (starts with sk_live_) that grants access to all Stripe API resources. To protect your business, use restricted API keys instead.
181: Your API keys carry many privileges. Follow best practices to keep your keys safe. Don’t embed secret or restricted API keys in source code or client-side applications. Instead, use your server platform’s secrets vault to provide keys to your server-side applications. If your platform doesn’t offer a secrets vault, set your keys in environment variables.
182: For added security, Workload Identity Federation lets your service authenticate without storing a long-lived API key. Your service exchanges a short-lived identity token from its cloud provider for a Stripe access token that expires after 1 hour.
183: The Stripe API authenticates requests using HTTP Basic Auth. Provide your API key as the basic auth username value. You don’t need to provide a password.
184: If you need to authenticate using bearer auth (for example, for a cross-origin request), use -H "Authorization: Bearer sk_test_...sk_test_..." instead of -u sk_test_...sk_test_....
185: Make all API requests over HTTPS. Calls made over plain HTTP fail. API requests without authentication also fail.
186: Was this section helpful?YesNo
187: Authenticated Request
188: curl https://api.stripe.com/v1/charges \
189: -u sk_test_...sk_test_...:
190: # The colon prevents curl from asking for a password.
191: Your API key
192: A sample test API key is included in all the examples here, so you can test any example right away. Do not submit any personally identifiable information in requests made with this key.
193: To test requests using your account, replace the sample API key with your actual API key or log in.
194: Errors
195: Ask about this section
196: Copy for LLM
197: View as Markdown
198: Stripe uses conventional HTTP response codes to indicate the success or failure of an API request. In general:
199: Codes in the 2xx range indicate success.
200: Codes in the 4xx range indicate an error that failed given the information provided. For example, an omitted required parameter, a failed charge, or a declined card.
201: Many of these include an error code that briefly explains the error reported.
202: See Error handling for guidance.
203: Codes in the 5xx range indicate an error with the Stripe servers (these are rare).
204: Was this section helpful?YesNo
205: Attributes
206: codenullable string
207: For some errors that could be handled programmatically, a short string indicating the error code reported.
208: decline_codenullable string
209: For card errors resulting from a card issuer decline, a short string indicating the card issuer’s reason for the decline if they provide one.
210: messagenullable string
211: A human-readable message providing more details about the error. For card errors, these messages can be shown to your users.
212: paramnullable string
213: If the error is parameter-specific, the parameter related to the error. For example, you can use this to display a message near the correct form field.
214: payment_intentnullable object
215: The PaymentIntent object for errors returned on a request involving a PaymentIntent.
216: typeenum
217: The type of error returned. One of api_error, card_error, idempotency_error, or invalid_request_error
218: Possible enum values
219: api_error
220: card_error
221: idempotency_error
222: invalid_request_error
223: More
224: Expand all
225: advice_codenullable string
226: chargenullable string
227: doc_urlnullable string
228: network_advice_codenullable string
229: network_decline_codenullable string
230: payment_methodnullable object
231: payment_method_typenullable string
232: request_log_urlnullable string
233: setup_intentnullable object
234: sourcenullable object
235: HTTP Status Code Summary
236: 200OKEverything worked as expected.
237: 400Bad RequestThe request was unacceptable, often due to missing a required parameter.
238: 401UnauthorizedNo valid API key provided.
239: 402Request FailedThe parameters were valid but the request failed.
240: 403ForbiddenThe API key doesn’t have permissions to perform the request.
241: 404Not FoundThe requested resource doesn’t exist.
242: 409ConflictThe request conflicts with another request (perhaps due to using the same idempotent key).
243: 424External Dependency FailedThe request couldn’t be completed due to a failure in a dependency external to Stripe.
244: 429Too Many RequestsToo many requests hit the API too quickly. We recommend an exponential backoff of your requests.
245: 500, 502, 503, 504Server ErrorsSomething went wrong on Stripe’s end. (These are rare.)
246: Error Types
247: api_errorAPI errors cover any other type of problem (e.g., a temporary problem with Stripe’s servers), and are extremely uncommon.
248: card_errorCard errors are the most common type of error you should expect to handle. They result when the user enters a card that can’t be charged for some reason.
249: idempotency_errorIdempotency errors occur when an Idempotency-Key is re-used on a request that does not match the first request’s API endpoint and parameters.
250: invalid_request_errorInvalid request errors arise when your request has invalid parameters.

87: Use API keys to authenticate API requests.
88: Ask about this page
89: Copy for LLM
90: View as Markdown
91: Set up agent
92: Stripe uses API keys to authenticate requests from your integration and determine which Stripe resources it can access. Choose the key type that matches where your code runs and grant server-side keys only the permissions your integration needs.
93: Use the API keys page in the Dashboard to create, reveal, expire and rotate keys for the account or sandbox you’re viewing. This guide covers keys used with the Stripe API. To learn about API v2 endpoints, behaviour and testing, see the API v2 overview.
94: If a request doesn’t include a valid key, Stripe returns an invalid request error. If a request includes an expired key, Stripe returns an authentication error. Use Workbench request logs to inspect API requests and troubleshoot errors.
95: If you're new to Stripe
96: Keep your business safe: Read our best practices for managing keys.
97: Build and test: Create or select a sandbox and use its test keys. For new integrations, use a separate general sandbox so settings and data remain isolated from live mode. Sandbox keys start with pk_test_ for publishable keys, rk_test_ for restricted keys, and sk_test_ for secret keys.
98: When you’re ready to accept real payments: Switch to your live mode keys, which start with pk_live_, rk_live_, and sk_live_.
99: If you need to find a webhook signing secret: Webhook secrets are separate from API keys. Find them in the Webhooks section of the Dashboard under each webhook endpoint.
100: Key types
101: Stripe supports the following API key types:
102: TypeSafe to exposeDescription
103: Publishable API key pk_...YesAPI key for Stripe.js, Elements and mobile SDKs. It can identify your account and create tokens or PaymentMethods from payment details, but it can’t perform sensitive operations such as creating charges or reading account data. You can include it in front-end code or applications you distribute.
104: Restricted API key (RAK) rk_...NoAPI key with permissions you control. Limit the damage to your business that a fraudulent actor could cause if they obtained your key. Create as many RAKs as you want and assign them to different parts of your application. Stripe Apps can also use RAK authentication to generate a permissioned key when a user installs an app. This guide explains how to configure and use RAKs.
105: Secret API key sk_...NoAPI key that has unrestricted permissions on all Stripe APIs. Because you can’t limit their permissions, we don’t recommend using secret keys for new use cases, and for existing integrations, we recommend migrating secret key usage to RAKs.
106: Organisation API key sk_org_...NoAPI key that works at the organisation level. Same as account-level restricted or secret keys, but operates at the organisation level to manage multiple Stripe accounts at once. This guide explains how to configure and use organisation API keys.
107: We also support managed API keys issued by certain hosting platforms. Managed keys are secret API keys that a hosting platform delivers directly to your hosted applications. You don’t need to handle managed keys directly; your hosting provider issues and rotates them for you.
108: Webhook signing secrets
109: Webhook signing secrets aren’t API keys – they’re per-webhook secrets that your webhook receiver uses to authenticate that webhooks actually came from Stripe. You can find the signing secret for each webhook endpoint in the Webhooks section of the Dashboard.
110: You’re responsible for managing your API keys safely. Read our guide to best practice for protecting API keys.
111: Sandbox versus live mode
112: All Stripe API requests occur in either a ‘‘sandbox’’ or ‘‘live mode’’. You can use a sandbox to test your integration and access test data, and live mode to access actual account data. Each mode has its own set of API keys, and objects in one mode aren’t accessible to the other. For example, a sandbox product object can’t be part of a live mode payment.
113: TypeWhen to useObjectsHow to useConsiderations
114: SandboxesUse a sandbox, and its associated test API keys, as you build your integration. In a sandbox, card networks and payment providers don’t process payments.API calls return simulated objects. For example, you can retrieve and use test Customer, PaymentIntent, Refund and Subscription objects.Use test credit cards and accounts. You can’t accept real payment methods or work with real accounts.Identity doesn’t perform any verification checks. Also, Connect account objects don’t return sensitive fields.
115: Live modeUse live mode, and its associated live API keys, when you’re ready to launch your integration and accept real money. In live mode, card networks and payment providers do process payments.API calls return real objects. For example, you can retrieve and use real Customer, PaymentIntent, Refund and Subscription objects.Accept real credit cards and work with customer accounts. You can accept actual payment authorisations, charges, and captures for credit cards and accounts.Disputes have a more nuanced flow and a simpler testing process. Also, some payment methods have a more nuanced flow and require more steps.
116: API keys for autonomous agents
117: When you create a restricted API key, you can tag it as belonging to an autonomous agent, an AI system that operates independently to complete tasks such as processing refunds or managing subscriptions. To tag a key as an agent key, select Authorising agent access to your account when Stripe prompts you for the key’s intended use during creation.
118: Agent-tagged keys work the same as other restricted API keys for authentication and permissions.
119: The difference is in governance: agent-tagged keys are automatically subject to approval rules, which require a designated reviewer to approve sensitive actions before they take effect. Stripe provides a set of default rules when you create your first agent-tagged key. These rules cover high-risk actions such as payouts, refunds and account configuration changes.
120: This is the recommended way to give autonomous agents access to your Stripe account. The approval rules act as a safeguard against agent mistakes, unexpected behaviour and hallucinations – giving you visibility and control without blocking agents from doing their jobs.
121: Protect your keys
122: Only publishable keys are safe to expose outside your application’s back end. You’re responsible for protecting other Stripe API keys, including restricted API keys. To protect your keys:
123: Store sensitive keys in a secrets vault provided by your hosting platform. This blog post offers an example. If you can’t use a secrets vault, use environment variables to provide keys to your back end applications.
124: Don’t put keys in source code or configuration files checked into version control.
125: Configure access policies so keys can only be used from your known servers.
126: Rotate keys when team members with access to the keys leave your organisation.
127: Don’t share keys over email, chat or other unencrypted channels.
128: For a comprehensive guide, see best practice for managing secret API keys. We also maintain a library of skills to help AI agents follow these best practices.
129: Manage your API keys
130: The following sections describe how to create and manage keys on the API keys page.
131: Create a restricted API key
132: Use restricted API keys (RAKs) for most use cases. You can use a RAK to assign the exact permissions your integration needs, which can help reduce the damage a fraudulent actor could cause to your business if they obtained your key.
133: Follow the instructions on Restricted API Keys to create a RAK, configure its permissions, and migrate from secret keys.
134: Create a secret API key
135: Create an unrestricted secret API key only when your integration requires access to all Stripe APIs and resources without restriction. If a fraudulent actor obtains your secret key, they can harm your business. We recommend using RAKs instead.
136: On the API keys page, click Create secret key.
137: In the dialog, enter the verification code that we send you by email or text message. If the dialog doesn’t continue automatically, click Continue.
138: Enter a name in the Key name field, then click Create.
139: Click the key value to copy it.
140: Save the key value. In live mode, you can’t retrieve it later.
141: In the Add a note field, enter the location where you saved the key, then click Done.
142: Reveal an API key
143: When you create a secret key in live mode, Stripe displays it one time before you save it. Copy the key before you save it because you can’t reveal it later. We can’t recover keys that you’ve forgotten or lost access to. If you lose a key, rotate or delete it and create another. In live mode, you can reveal only API keys that Stripe creates for you, such as a default secret key or a key generated by a scheduled rotation. In sandbox mode, you can always see all of your API keys, including restricted and secret keys. Publishable API keys aren’t sensitive, so we show them by default and you don’t need to do anything to reveal them.
144: Security tip
145: Store sensitive keys in a place where you won’t lose them, such as a secrets vault provided by your platform. Don’t put keys in your application’s code.
146: Reveal a RAK in live mode
147: You can reveal only live-mode RAKs that we created for you. If you create a RAK yourself, you can’t reveal it after you’ve seen it once.
148: On the API keys page in live mode, in the Restricted keys list, click Reveal live key for the key you want to reveal.
149: Click the key value to copy it.
150: Save the key value in your platform’s secrets vault. If your platform doesn’t provide one, use an environment variable.
151: Click Hide live key.
152: Reveal a secret API key in live mode
153: You can reveal only live-mode secret keys that we created for you. If you create a secret key yourself, you can’t reveal it after you’ve seen it once.
154: On the API keys page in live mode, in the Standard keys list, click Reveal live key for the key you want to reveal.
155: Click the key value to copy it.
156: Save the key value in your platform’s secrets vault. If your platform doesn’t provide one, use an environment variable.
157: Click Hide live key.
158: Click the overflow menu (), then select Edit key for the key you want to add a note to.
159: In the Note field, enter the location where you saved the key, then click Save.
160: Limit an API key to certain IP addresses
161: Access policies have replaced IP address restrictions. Use policies, not restrictions.
162: Change an API key’s name or note
163: On the API keys page, click the overflow menu () for the key you want to change.
164: Select Edit key.
165: Do the following:
166: To change the name, enter a new name in the Key name field.
167: To change the note text, enter the new note text in the Note field.
168: Click Save.
169: Expire an API key
170: If you expire a secret API key or a restricted API key, you must create a new one and update any code that uses the expired key. Code that uses the expired key can no longer make API calls.
171: Note
172: You can’t expire a publishable key.
173: On the API keys page, in the Restricted keys or Standard keys list, click the overflow menu () for the key you want to expire.
174: Select Expire key.
175: In the dialog, click Expire key. If you no longer want to expire the key, click Cancel.
176: Rotate an API key
177: Rotating an API key revokes it and generates a replacement key that’s ready to use immediately. You can also schedule an API key to rotate after a certain time. The replacement key is named as follows:
178: The replacement publishable key name is always Publishable key.
179: The replacement secret key name is always Secret key.
180: The replacement restricted key name is the same as the rotated key.
181: You can rename a secret or restricted API key by editing the key.
182: Rotate an API key in scenarios such as:
183: If you lose a secret or restricted API key in live mode and you can’t recover it from the Dashboard.
184: If a secret or restricted API key is compromised and you need to revoke it to block any potentially malicious API requests that might use the key.
185: If a team member with access to the key leaves your organisation or changes roles.
186: If your policy requires rotating keys at certain intervals.
187: Rotate safely to avoid downtime
188: To avoid downtime during key rotation:
189: Use the grace period: When you rotate a key in the Dashboard, both the old and new keys work for up to 7 days. This lets you migrate gradually without downtime. If you need more than 7 days, create a new key manually, migrate to it, then expire the old one when you’re done.
190: Roll out gradually: If possible, use the new key from a small subset of your servers or services first, and watch your server logs for errors before deploying further.
191: Monitor before revoking: Before the old key expires, check its request logs, and expire it only after its request volume has been at zero for a few hours or days.
192: Rotate an API key in the Dashboard
193: On the API keys page, click the overflow menu () for the key you want to rotate.
194: Select Rotate key.
195: Select an expiry date from the Expiry dropdown. If you choose Now, the old key is deleted. If you specify a time, the remaining time until the key expires displays below the key name.
196: Click Rotate API key.
197: Click the key value to copy it.
198: Save the key value. In live mode, you can’t retrieve it later.
199: In the Add a note field, enter the location where you saved the key, then click Save or Done.
200: Restore an API key’s access
201: An API key might have its access limited if it hasn’t been used to create transfers, payouts or update payout destinations for over 180 days. You can’t use a limited access key to create payouts and transfers or to create payout destinations. You can restore access to use the key normally or to perform a blocked action.
202: Restore access for an API key
203: On the API keys page, click the overflow menu () for the key you want to restore.
204: Select Restore access.
205: Click Restore.
206: View API request logs for a key
207: To open the API request logs, click the overflow menu () for any key, then select View request logs. Opening the logs redirects you to Workbench in the Stripe Dashboard.
208: Switch to live mode
209: When you’re ready to accept real payments, use live mode API keys instead of sandbox keys. On the API keys page, toggle from sandbox mode to live mode. The page now shows your live mode API keys.
210: Complete go-live checklist
211: Switching API keys is only one step. Review the full go-live checklist to make sure your integration is production ready.
212: Publishable keys (client-side)
213: Copy your live mode publishable key (starts with pk_live_) and replace the pk_test_ key in your client-side code. It’s safe to embed this key in your code or apps.
214: Restricted or secret API keys (server-side)
215: Server-side API keys are sensitive, so review our best practice for managing secret API keys. We recommend generating restricted API keys for your server-side code to limit the damage to your business if your keys are ever exposed or compromised.
216: Before you start using a live mode key in your back-end application, remove any hardcoded API keys from your code. Instead, use a secrets vault to supply the sandbox key, and confirm that your application still works. If your platform doesn’t provide a secrets vault, you can use an environment variable.
217: Reveal and copy your live mode keys (which start with rk_live_ or sk_live_). Store the key value securely in your server environment.
218: Configure your server environment to supply live mode keys instead of sandbox keys to your application.
219: Webhook signing keys (server-side)
220: If you use webhooks, update each webhook endpoint’s URL and copy the new signing secret from the Webhooks section of the Dashboard.
221: Access policies
222: You can restrict access to a key by attaching an access policy to it. If someone attempts a request using a key they can’t access, Stripe blocks the request and notifies you.
223: Stripe recommends configuring access policies on all live mode keys. That notifies you of any unauthorised access, so you can rotate the keys accordingly.
224: You can manage access by assigning different policies to different keys. For example, you can distinguish between staging and production environments by assigning different policies to their respective keys.
225: Access policy types
226: Stripe supports the following types of access policies:
227: IP addresses: Restrict access to one or more specific IPv4 addresses or CIDR ranges. Use this approach if your servers have fixed IP addresses.
228: Advanced: Restrict access by Autonomous System Number (ASN), country and common threat categories. If you’re dynamically scaling, you can provide access to your cloud provider using the ASN and country.
229: An advanced access policy can use any combination of the following rules:
230: ASNs to allow: Requests from specified ASNs are allowed; all others are blocked.
231: Countries: Requests from specified countries are allowed; all others are blocked.
232: Sources: Requests from selected sources are blocked. You can select the following sources:
233: Anonymous VPNs: Third-party VPN services sold for privacy and anonymity (not including corporate VPNs). Consider blocking these if you don’t use VPNs to access the Stripe API.
234: Public proxies: Open proxy servers from public lists. Consider blocking these if you don’t use public proxies to access the Stripe API.
235: Residential proxies: Proxies associated with residential ISPs. Consider blocking these if you don’t use residential ISPs to access the Stripe API.
236: Tor exit nodes: Traffic from the Tor network. Consider blocking these if you don’t access the Stripe API over Tor.
237: Selecting multiple rules combines them using AND logic. For example, if you allow ASN 16509 (Amazon), allow the United States, and block Tor exit nodes, then the policy only allows requests from AWS IPs in the US that are not known to be Tor exit nodes. It blocks all other requests.
238: Create an access policy
239: To create an access policy, go to the Access policies page in your Dashboard and follow these steps:
240: Click + Create policy.
241: Enter a name (for example, “Production servers”) and an optional description.
242: Select IP addresses or Advanced.
243: Depending on the selected type, configure the policy:
244: IP addresses: Enter one or more valid public IPv4 addresses or CIDR ranges. For example, 192.0.2.0/24 covers the range 192.0.2.0–192.0.2.255.
245: Advanced: Specify any combination of ASNs to allow, countries to allow and sources to block, as described in Access policy types.
246: Click Next.
247: Review the policy details, then click Create policy.
248: If prompted to authenticate, follow the on-screen instructions.
249: If the creation succeeded, the new policy appears in the list.
250: Apply or remove an access policy
251: To apply an access policy to an API key, go to the API keys page in your Dashboard and follow these steps:
252: In the Standard keys or Restricted keys list, find the key you want to update and open its overflow menu ().
253: Select Manage access policy.
254: In the Access policy dropdown, select the policy you want.
255: Review the details of the selected policy, then click Save.
256: If prompted to authenticate, follow the on-screen instructions.
257: To remove an access policy from a key, go to the API keys page in your Dashboard and follow these steps:
258: In the Standard keys or Restricted keys list, find the key you want to update and open its overflow menu ().
259: Select Manage access policy.
260: In the Access policy dropdown, select None.
261: Click Save.
262: Update an access policy
263: To make changes to an access policy, go to the Access policies page in your Dashboard and follow these steps:
264: Find the policy you want to change, and open its overflow menu ().
265: Select Edit policy.
266: Update the policy options as described in Create an access policy, then click Next.
267: Review the policy details, then click Save.
268: If prompted to authenticate, follow the on-screen instructions.
269: When you update an access policy, the changes apply immediately to all API keys it’s assigned to.
270: Delete an access policy
271: To delete an access policy, go to the Access policies page in your Dashboard and follow these steps:
272: Find the policy you want to delete and open its overflow menu ().
273: Select Delete policy.
274: Review the confirmation dialogue to understand the impact, then click Delete policy.
275: Deleting an access policy immediately removes it from all API keys it was applied to. Those keys allow requests from any source until you apply another policy to them.

72: Set up agent
73: Test your integration in a sandbox by simulating transactions with test values – these transactions don’t move funds.
74: You can access your sandboxes using the account picker in the Dashboard.
75: Test cards act as “fake” credit cards, and allow you to simulate the following scenarios:
76: Successful payments by card brand or country
77: Card errors due to declines, fraud or invalid data
78: Disputes, including early fraud warnings, and refunds
79: Authentication with 3D Secure and PINs
80: You can also test non-card payments in a sandbox. Non-card payments are payment methods that aren’t credit or debit cards. Stripe supports various non-card payment options, such as digital wallets and bank transfers. Each payment method has its own special values.
81: If you’re testing a subscription integration, see Test your Billing integration.
82: Don’t use testing environments to load test your integration because you might hit rate limits. To load test your integration, see load testing.
83: How to use test cards
84: When you work with a test card, use test API keys in all API calls. This is true whether you’re serving a payment form to test interactively or writing test code.
85: Card-level state from one test can affect later tests that use the same card. When a test depends on card-level state, use a different test card for each independent end-to-end scenario.
86: Don't use real card details
87: Don’t use real card details. The Stripe Services Agreement prohibits testing in live mode using real payment method details. Use your test API keys and the card numbers below.
88: Testing interactively
89: When testing interactively, use a card number, such as 4242 4242 4242 4242. Enter the card number in the Dashboard or in any payment form.
90: Use a valid future date, such as 12/34.
91: Use any three-digit CVC (four digits for American Express cards).
92: Use any value you like for other form fields.
93: Test code
94: When writing test code, use a PaymentMethod such as pm_card_visa instead of a card number. We don’t recommend using card numbers directly in API calls or server-side code, even in testing environments. If you use them, your code might not be PCI-compliant when you go live. By default, a PaymentMethod isn’t attached to a Customer.

Don’t store keys in source code or configuration files checked into version control. To learn how to use live keys safely, see Best practices for managing secret API keys.

226: Simulate customer location with email
227: When testing Checkout Sessions, Payment Links or pricing tables, you can simulate a customer’s geographic location by using a location-formatted email address. Add a +location_XX suffix to the local part of any email address, where XX is a valid two-letter ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country code.

477: Test settlement behaviour
478: Test transactions settle instantly and are added to your available test balance. This behaviour differs from live mode, where transactions can take multiple days to settle in your available balance.
479: Test asynchronous payment methods
480: Asynchronous, or “delayed notification”, payment methods don’t immediately confirm whether a payment succeeds or fails. After your customer submits payment details, the PaymentIntent can enter a processing state. The final outcome, such as succeeded or requires_payment_method, arrives later, from a few minutes in a sandbox to several working days in live mode.
481: This behaviour differs from most card payments, which usually receive an immediate authorisation response from the issuer.
482: Don’t rely on a client-side callback or redirect to determine the final status for these payment methods. Always use webhooks to drive fulfilment.
483: Understand the PaymentIntent lifecycle
484: Payment methods that don’t require further action from your customer to authorise the payment, such as bank debits, move through these states after your customer submits payment:
485: StepStateDescription
486: 1processingYour customer submitted the payment, and the outcome isn’t yet known.
487: 2asucceededThe payment is confirmed.
488: 2brequires_payment_methodThe payment failed, for example because of insufficient funds or a closed account.
489: Payment methods that require further action from your customer to authorise the payment, such as voucher-based methods including Multibanco, Boleto, OXXO, and Konbini, add an earlier state before processing:
490: StepStateDescription
491: 1requires_actionStripe issued a voucher or payment code and is waiting for your customer to pay out of band.
492: 2processingStripe is waiting for the final outcome, and your customer can no longer complete the voucher payment through the original flow.
493: 3asucceededYour customer paid the voucher.
494: 3brequires_payment_methodThe voucher expired or the payment failed.

499: payment_intent.succeededThe payment is confirmed.Fulfil the order.
500: payment_intent.payment_failedThe payment failed, such as for insufficient funds, an expired voucher, or a closed account.Notify your customer and request a new payment method.
501: payment_intent.requires_actionStripe issued a voucher or out-of-band action and is waiting for your customer. This applies to Multibanco, Boleto, OXXO and Konbini.Send your customer the voucher or payment instructions.
502: payment_intent.canceledThe PaymentIntent was cancelled before your customer completed payment.Notify your customer. Don’t fulfil the order.

574: Submit the payment to Stripe.
575: Authorise or fail the test payment.
576: Make sure that the page (corresponding to return_url) on your website provides the status of the payment.

59: Set up agent
60: To securely set up your account:
61: Create a Stripe account if you haven’t already.
62: Complete the account checklist for safety and security compliance.
63: Verify your business in the Dashboard. Provide information about your business, product and relationship to the business. As you use more Stripe services, we might request additional information or verification.
64: Accounts used only for Stripe Apps
65: If you use your account only to build and test Stripe Apps without accepting payments, you don’t need to configure payment processing. Follow the account-security recommendations. To publish to the Stripe App Marketplace, you must activate your account with a verified email address and business details, and meet the Marketplace requirements and restrictions.
66: After creating a Stripe account, you can test Stripe services in a sandbox. To use a service in live mode, verify your business and complete its activation requirements.
67: Our “Know Your Customer” (KYC) obligations require us to collect and maintain this information for all users. Regulators and financial partners require it to help prevent financial-system abuse. We review it for compliance with our services agreement and contact you if we need anything else.
68: After activating a Stripe service on a live account, you can’t change the business origin country. To use a different supported country as your primary business location, create a new account.
69: Caution
70: Privacy and security are priorities for Stripe. Our privacy policy explains how and for what purposes we collect, use, retain, disclose, and safeguard any personal data you provide to us.
71: Public business information
72: Even if you don’t accept payments (for example, if you only plan to create and publish Stripe Apps), you must provide business information to verify your business.
73: If you accept payments, your customers see the following details on either their card statements or in email receipts sent by Stripe.
74: Business name and website URL
75: Support email address, phone number and address
76: Support site URL
77: Statement descriptor text
78: You provide this information when you verify your business, and can update it any time in your Account settings. Make sure that your statement descriptor text and business information are clearly associated with you. If your customer can’t recognise one of your payments, they might dispute it.
79: Keep your account safe
80: After you set up your account, you’ll want to keep it safe. Here are our recommendations:
81: Keep private information private: Don’t share your password and keep your secret API keys confidential on your own servers. Store secret keys in a secrets vault, not in source code. Use restricted API keys instead of secret keys wherever possible. As a reminder, Stripe employees never ask you for your keys.
82: Don’t reuse your Stripe password: Use a password that’s unique to Stripe. If you use your password on another site and that site is compromised, an attacker could use those stolen credentials to take over your account. If you need to reset your password, click Edit > Change password in your Personal details settings and enter a new password.
83: Use team members to provide others with access to your account: You can invite others (with limited access) to your Stripe account so that they can log in and take certain actions.
84: Update your computer and browser regularly: We recommend configuring your computer to automatically download and install updates (for example, macOS or Windows). This helps protect your system against automated attacks and malware.
85: Beware of phishing: All genuine Stripe sites use the stripe.com domain and HTTPS. If you get an email from us that you don’t expect, go directly to our site to log in. Don’t enter your password after clicking a link in an email. If you’re not sure if a message is from Stripe, review Verified Stripe domains on Stripe Support.
86: Enable two-factor authentication with a passkey or security key: When you enable two-factor authentication (2FA), you need to provide an additional verification step to complete the login process. Stripe supports passkeys, security keys, authenticator apps and SMS. We recommend passkeys or security keys because they’re resistant to phishing. SMS-based 2FA is vulnerable to SIM-swapping and interception, so use it only as a last resort. To enable this feature, go to your user settings.
87: Close your account
88: You can close your account any time you want. We recommend you leave it dormant in case you need to access any financial data or take action to resolve a dispute.

64: Let your AI agents interact with the Stripe API by using our MCP server.
65: Ask about this page
66: Copy for LLM

68: Set up agent
69: The Stripe Model Context Protocol (MCP) server provides tools that AI agents can use to interact with the Stripe API and search the Stripe knowledge base, including documentation and support articles.
70: Set up Stripe MCP with a plugin Recommended
71: Agent plugins for Stripe automatically configure the Stripe MCP server, install our skills and make sure they’re up to date. You get our latest capabilities without configuration or maintenance.
72: Install the Stripe CLI using the installation script for your operating system. Script installations enable automatic updates by default.
73: On macOS or Linux:
74: Command Line
75: curl -fsSL https://cli.stripe.com/install.sh | sh
76: export PATH="$HOME/.stripe/bin:$PATH"
77: On Windows, run the following command in PowerShell:
78: irm https://cli.stripe.com/install.ps1 | iex
79: After installation, open a new terminal and install the agent tooling:
80: Command Line
81: stripe agent setup
82: This command automatically detects which agents you use, and runs the applicable commands.
83: Manually set up Stripe MCP
84: If your MCP client doesn’t support agent plugins for Stripe, or you prefer to configure the Stripe MCP server and install the skills manually, follow these instructions:
85: Cursor
86: Claude Code
87: Claude Desktop
88: Codex
89: ChatGPT
90: VS Code
91: Other
92: Install in Cursor
93: Select Install in Cursor to open Cursor and add the Stripe MCP server. To configure it manually, add the following configuration to ~/.cursor/mcp.json.
94: For more information, see Cursor’s MCP documentation.
95: {
96: "mcpServers": {
97: "stripe": {
98: "url": "https://mcp.stripe.com"
99: }
100: }
101: }
102: Manage MCP access and sessions
103: Stripe’s MCP server supports two authentication methods:
104: OAuth: Use OAuth when a client accesses Stripe on behalf of your Stripe user account.
105: Agent API keys: Use an agent API key when an AI application needs independent, persistent access to Stripe.
106: When you connect an MCP client with OAuth, the client opens Stripe’s OAuth consent page. You can grant access to one or more live mode accounts or sandboxes and set different permissions for each environment. See the MCP authorisation specification for details.
107: OAuth session expiry
108: OAuth refresh tokens expire after 14 days, and refreshing tokens doesn’t extend the session beyond 14 days from your initial authorisation. When your session expires, reconnect your MCP client to Stripe and authorise it again.
109: If your organisation manages your device or network, your IT administrator might block connections to external MCP servers. When the Stripe MCP server doesn’t connect in a managed environment, ask your IT department to allow mcp.stripe.com.
110: Manage MCP access for all team members
111: If you’re an administrator, you can enable or disable MCP access for your entire team in the Dashboard. Configure access separately for live mode and sandbox environments.
112: Manage your sessions
113: Your authorised MCP clients appear under OAuth sessions in your user settings. To revoke a session:
114: Find the client in the OAuth sessions list.
115: Click the overflow menu ().
116: Select Revoke access.
117: Manage sessions as an administrator
118: To view or revoke another user’s sessions, your role must include permissions to manage team members. The Administrator role includes these permissions.
119: Open Team and security in the Dashboard.
120: Select the team member you want to manage.
121: Find the OAuth sessions table.
122: To revoke one session, click its overflow menu and select Revoke access. To revoke every listed session, select Revoke all.
123: Session management applies only to the account or organisation and environment – live mode or a sandbox – that you’re currently viewing. Revoking a session removes access only within that scope. The session remains active for accounts outside your current scope.
124: When you view an organisation, the Accounts column shows the accounts associated with each session.
125: Authenticate Stripe MCP
126: Use OAuth for interactive MCP clients. OAuth lets you authorise and revoke a client without sharing an API key.
127: For autonomous clients that can’t use OAuth, create an agent API key with only the permissions the client needs. You can identify agent API keys in the Dashboard by the Agent badge. Pass the agent API key as the bearer token in the Authorization header of your request. If you’re replacing an existing key, test the new configuration in a sandbox, then expire the old key.
128: Update API key authentication before January 11, 2027
129: Starting January 11, 2027, Stripe MCP will no longer accept full-access secret keys or non-agent restricted API keys. Migrate to an agent API key or reconnect with OAuth before that date. Requests using an unsupported key receive a 401 response with an OAuth discovery challenge.
130: Tools
131: The server exposes the following MCP tools.
132: Turn on your MCP client’s tool-approval setting so you can review tool calls before they run, and exercise caution when using the Stripe MCP with other servers to avoid prompt injection attacks. If you have feedback or want to see more tools, email us at mcp@stripe.com.

136: stripe_api_readRead data with any Stripe API GET method
137: stripe_api_writeWrite data with any Stripe API POST, PATCH, PUT and DELETE method
138: Accountget_stripe_account_infoRetrieve account

142: Build SQL queries based on natural language

144: Treasury Public previewget_balance_summaryDisplays an interactive balance summary across the Stripe balance and Treasury accounts

152: To prepare a company incorporation application, ask your assistant:
153: Help me prepare a Stripe Atlas application for a Delaware C corporation with two founders. Check for an existing application before creating one.
154: You review documents, pay, sign and submit in the Dashboard. See Prepare an Atlas application with an agent or CLI.
155: The Stripe MCP server exposes multiple APIs that you can call with the stripe_api_read and stripe_api_write tools. This access makes much of the API available through MCP without increasing the context window unnecessarily.
156: Supported API methods
157: Confirm actions by agents acting on your behalf
158: When you connect an AI agent to Stripe through the MCP server using your user credentials, you authorise the agent to access data and take actions in Stripe on your behalf.
159: Before an agent completes certain actions on your behalf, Stripe can require you to review and approve the request in the Dashboard. Look for the Human confirmation badge beside action descriptions in the Tools reference and Supported API methods.
160: Your MCP client displays tool names that can group multiple actions. For example, creating a refund uses stripe_api_write, which also supports other actions that don’t use this confirmation flow. Confirmation depends on the action, not only the tool name.
161: Stripe’s confirmation requirement is separate from your MCP client’s tool-approval setting. Account-specific approval rules can require review of additional actions.
162: To confirm an action, click the URL provided by your agent and review the details of the request.
163: Confirm a refund request
164: When you click Approve, Stripe provides the agent with an approval token, but you need to tell the agent to retry the operation, which doesn’t require human confirmation. If you don’t approve the action within 24 hours, it expires.
165: Use MCP with connected accounts
166: By default, Stripe MCP tools operate on the Stripe account associated with your OAuth session or API key. If you only need your agent to work with your platform account, manually set up Stripe MCP.
167: If you’re a Connect platform, you can also use MCP to retrieve or update resources for your connected accounts. For example, a support agent could retrieve a customer or investigate a payment for a specific connected account.
168: MCP doesn’t support OAuth when acting on behalf of connected accounts. Instead, authenticate with an agent API key for your platform and grant only the connected-account permissions that your agent needs.
169: To make an MCP call as a connected account, pass the Stripe-Account header. This is useful when you provide an agent that allows your connected accounts to make MCP calls through your platform.
170: {
171: "mcpServers": {
172: "stripe": {
173: "url": "https://mcp.stripe.com",
174: "headers": {
175: "Authorization": "Bearer {{AGENT_API_KEY}}",
176: "Stripe-Account": "acct_xxxxxxxxx"
177: }
178: }
179: }
180: }

This chat may be logged for quality and training purposes. Please don't send Bill any PII -- he's scared of intimacy. All chats with Bill are subject to Plaid's Privacy Policy.
69: API Reference
70: Comprehensive reference for integrating with Plaid API endpoints
71: API endpoints and webhooks
72: For documentation on specific API endpoints and webhooks, use the navigation menu or search.
73: API access
74: To gain access to the Plaid API, create an account on the Plaid Dashboard. Once you've completed the signup process and acknowledged our terms, we'll provide a live client_id and secret via the Dashboard.
75: API protocols and headers
76: The Plaid API is JSON over HTTP. Requests are POST requests, and responses are JSON, with errors indicated in response bodies as error_code and error_type (use these in preference to HTTP status codes for identifying application-level errors). All responses come as standard JSON, with a small subset returning binary data where appropriate. The Plaid API is served over HTTPS TLS v1.2 to ensure data privacy; HTTP and HTTPS with TLS versions other than 1.2 are not supported. Clients must use an up to date root certificate bundle as the only TLS verification path; certificate pinning should never be used. All requests must include a Content-Type of application/json and the body must be valid JSON.
77: Almost all Plaid API endpoints require a client_id and secret. These may be sent either in the request body or in the headers PLAID-CLIENT-ID and PLAID-SECRET.
78: Every Plaid API response includes a request_id, either in the body or (in the case of endpoints that return binary data, such as /asset_report/pdf/get) in the response headers. For faster support, include the request_id when contacting support regarding a specific API call.
79: API host
80: https://sandbox.plaid.com (Sandbox)
81: https://production.plaid.com (Production)
82: Plaid has two environments: Sandbox and Production. Items cannot be moved between environments. The Sandbox environment supports only test Items. You can request Production API access via the Dashboard.
83: API status and incidents
84: API status is available at status.plaid.com.
85: API status and incidents are also available programmatically via the following endpoints:
86: https://status.plaid.com/api/v2/status.json for current status
87: https://status.plaid.com/api/v2/incidents.json for current and historical incidents
88: For a complete list of all API status information available programmatically, as well as more information on using these endpoints, see the Incident.io Status API documentation.
89: For information on institution-specific insights, see Troubleshooting institution insights.
90: Storing API data
91: Any token returned by the API is sensitive and should be stored securely. Except for the public_token and link_token, all Plaid tokens are long-lasting and should never be exposed on the client side. Consumer data obtained from the Plaid API is sensitive information and should be managed accordingly. For guidance and best practices on how to store and handle sensitive data, see the Open Finance Data Security Standard.
92: Identifiers used by the Plaid API that do not contain consumer data and are not keys or tokens are designed for usage in less sensitive contexts. The most common of these identifiers are the account_id, item_id, link_session_id, and request_id. These identifiers are commonly used for logging and debugging purposes.
93: API field formats
94: Strings
95: Many string fields returned by Plaid APIs are reported exactly as returned by the financial institution. For this reason, Plaid does not have maximum length limits or standardized formats for strings returned by the API. In practice, field lengths of 280 characters will generally be adequate for storing returned strings, although Plaid does not guarantee this as a maximum string length.
96: Numbers and money
97: Plaid returns all currency values as decimal values in dollars (or the equivalent for the currency being used), rather than as integers. In some cases, it may be possible for a money value returned by the Plaid API to have more than two digits of precision -- this is common, for example, when reporting crypto balances.
98: OpenAPI definition file
99: OpenAPI is a standard format for describing RESTful APIs that allows those APIs to be integrated with tools for a wide variety of applications, including testing, client library generation, IDE integration, and more. The Plaid API is specified in our Plaid OpenAPI GitHub repo.
100: Postman collection
101: The Postman collection is a convenient tool for exploring Plaid API endpoints without writing code. The Postman collection provides pre-formatted requests for almost all of Plaid's API endpoints. All you have to do is fill in your API keys and any arguments. To get started, check out the Plaid Postman Collection Quickstart on GitHub.
102: Client libraries
103: See the client libraries page for more information on Plaid's client libraries.

53: Quickstart setup

73: Create your first Item
74: Most API requests interact with an Item, which is a Plaid term for a login at a financial institution. A single end-user of your application might have accounts at different financial institutions, which means they would have multiple different Items. An Item is not the same as a financial institution account, although every account will be associated with an Item. For example, if a user has one login at their bank that allows them to access both their checking account and their savings account, a single Item would be associated with both of those accounts.
75: Now that you have the Quickstart running, you'll add your first Item in the Sandbox environment. Once you've opened the Quickstart app on localhost, click the Launch Link button and select any institution. Use the Sandbox credentials to simulate a successful login.
76: Sandbox credentials
77: username: user_good
78: password: pass_good
79: If prompted to enter a 2FA code: 1234
80: Once you have entered your credentials and moved to the next screen, you have created your first Item! You can now make API calls for that Item by using the buttons in the Quickstart. In the next section, we'll explain what actually happened and how the Quickstart works.
81: How it works
82: As you might have noticed, you use both a server and a client-side component to
83: access the Plaid APIs. The flow looks like this:
84: The Plaid flow begins when your user wants to connect their bank account to your app.
85: 1Call /link/token/create to create a link_token and pass the temporary token to your app's client.
86: 2Use the link_token to open Link for your user. In the onSuccess callback, Link will provide a temporary public_token. This token can also be obtained on the backend via /link/token/get.
87: 3Call /item/public_token/exchange to exchange the public_token for a permanent access_token and item_id for the new Item.
88: 4Store the access_token and use it to make product requests for your user's Item.
89: The first step is to create a new link_token by making a /link/token/create request and passing in the required configurations. This link_token is a short-lived, one-time use token that authenticates your app with Plaid Link, our frontend module. Several of the environment variables you configured when launching the Quickstart, such as PLAID_PRODUCTS, are used as parameters for the link_token.
90: /link/token/create
91: Node▼
92: app.post('/api/create_link_token', async function (request, response) {
93: // Get the client_user_id by searching for the current user
94: const user = await User.find(...);
95: const clientUserId = user.id;
96: const linkTokenRequest = {
97: user: {
98: // This should correspond to a unique id for the current user.
99: client_user_id: clientUserId,
100: },
101: client_name: 'Plaid Test App',
102: products: ['auth'],
103: language: 'en',
104: webhook: 'https://webhook.example.com',
105: redirect_uri: 'https://domainname.com/oauth-page.html',
106: country_codes: ['US'],
107: };
108: try {
109: const createTokenResponse = await client.linkTokenCreate(linkTokenRequest);
110: response.json(createTokenResponse.data);
111: } catch (error) {
112: // handle error
113: }
114: });
115: Once you have a link_token, you can use it to initialize Link. Link is a drop-in client-side module available for web, iOS, and Android that handles the authentication process. The Quickstart uses Plaid's optional React bindings for an integration that you trigger via your own client-side code. This is what your users use to log into their financial institution accounts.
116: After a user submits their credentials within Link, Link provides you with a public_token via the onSuccess callback. The code below shows how the Quickstart passes the public_token from client-side code to the server. Both React and vanilla JavaScript examples are shown.
117: Initialize Link
118: React▼
119: // APP COMPONENT
120: // Upon rendering of App component, make a request to create and
121: // obtain a link token to be used in the Link component
122: import React, { useEffect, useState } from 'react';
123: import { usePlaidLink } from 'react-plaid-link';
124: const App = () => {
125: const [linkToken, setLinkToken] = useState(null);
126: const generateToken = async () => {
127: const response = await fetch('/api/create_link_token', {
128: method: 'POST',
129: });
130: const data = await response.json();
131: setLinkToken(data.link_token);
132: };
133: useEffect(() => {
134: generateToken();
135: }, []);
136: return linkToken != null ? <Link linkToken={linkToken} /> : <></>;
137: };
138: // LINK COMPONENT
139: // Use Plaid Link and pass link token and onSuccess function
140: // in configuration to initialize Plaid Link
141: interface LinkProps {
142: linkToken: string | null;
143: }
144: const Link: React.FC<LinkProps> = (props: LinkProps) => {
145: const onSuccess = React.useCallback(async (public_token, metadata) => {
146: // send public_token to server
147: const response = await fetch('/api/set_access_token', {
148: method: 'POST',
149: headers: {
150: 'Content-Type': 'application/json',
151: },
152: body: JSON.stringify({ public_token }),
153: });
154: // Handle response ...
155: }, []);
156: const config: Parameters<typeof usePlaidLink>[0] = {
157: token: props.linkToken!,
158: onSuccess,
159: };
160: const { open, ready } = usePlaidLink(config);
161: return (
162: <button onClick={() => open()} disabled={!ready}>
163: Link account
164: </button>
165: );
166: };
167: export default App;
168: Next, on the server side, the Quickstart calls /item/public_token/exchange to obtain an access_token, as illustrated in the code excerpt below. The access_token uniquely identifies an Item and is a required argument for most Plaid API endpoints. In your own code, you'll need to securely store your access_token in order to make API requests for that Item.
169: /item/public_token/exchange
170: Node▼
171: app.post('/api/exchange_public_token', async function (
172: request,
173: response,
174: next,
175: ) {
176: const publicToken = request.body.public_token;
177: try {
178: const tokenResponse = await client.itemPublicTokenExchange({
179: public_token: publicToken,
180: });
181: // These values should be saved to a persistent database and
182: // associated with the currently signed-in user
183: const accessToken = tokenResponse.data.access_token;
184: const itemID = tokenResponse.data.item_id;
185: response.json({ public_token_exchange: 'complete' });
186: } catch (error) {
187: // handle error
188: }
189: });
190: Making API requests
191: Now that we've gone over the Link flow and token exchange process, we can explore what happens when you press a button in the Quickstart to make an API call. As an example, we'll look at the Quickstart's call to /accounts/get, which retrieves basic information, such as name and balance, about the accounts associated with an Item. The call is fairly straightforward and uses the access_token as a single argument to the Plaid client object.
192: /accounts/get
193: Node▼
194: app.get('/api/accounts', async function (request, response, next) {
195: try {
196: const accountsResponse = await client.accountsGet({
197: access_token: accessToken,
198: });
199: prettyPrintResponse(accountsResponse);
200: response.json(accountsResponse.data);
201: } catch (error) {
202: prettyPrintResponse(error);
203: return response.json(formatError(error.response));
204: }
205: });

274: Next steps
275: Congratulations, you have completed the Plaid Quickstart! From here, we invite you to modify the Quickstart code in order to get more practice with the Plaid API. There are a few directions you can go in now:

31: Sandbox overview
32: Use the Sandbox to quickly develop and test your app
33: API ReferenceQuickstart
34: Sandbox overview
35: The Plaid Sandbox is a free and fully-featured environment for application development and testing. All Plaid functionality of both the Plaid API and Plaid Link is supported in the Sandbox environment. A variety of test accounts and institutions are available to test against, and you can create an unlimited number of test Items. Sandbox API keys can be obtained in the Plaid Dashboard.
36: To explore a Plaid product without writing code first, use Sandbox Studio in the Dashboard. It runs Sandbox API calls for you and shows the full request and response, which is the fastest way to see what an endpoint returns before integrating against it.
37: The Sandbox environment provides capabilities for testing core use cases, but does not reflect the full scope and complexity of data that can exist in Production. After testing in Sandbox, it is recommended to test in Production using a Trial plan to ensure your application can handle institution-specific behaviors and real-world data before launching.
38: Using Sandbox
39: The Sandbox can be reached by sending HTTPS POST requests to the endpoints on the sandbox.plaid.com domain. In order to use the Sandbox with a client library, specify Sandbox as your environment when initializing.
40: The default username/password combination for all Sandbox institutions is user_good / pass_good.
41: Most products can be immediately tested in Sandbox with no extra configuration. Some products, such as Payment Initiation (UK and Europe), may require your account be specially enabled. If the product you want to test against is not available in Sandbox, file a request for access ticket via the Dashboard.
42: Bypassing Link
43: Because the Link UI can and will change from time to time, it is not recommended to write automated end-to-end tests that exercise the Link UI. You should always bypass Link if you are writing an automated test suite that can block your build.
44: When doing repeated manual tests, or for writing automated tests against Sandbox, completing the Link flow may be impractical. As an alternative, you can also create Items in Sandbox via the API, using a special Sandbox-only endpoint, /sandbox/public_token/create. This endpoint allows you to generate a public_token for an arbitrary institution ID, initial products, and test credentials.
45: Simulating data and events
46: The Sandbox provides rich test data, as well as the ability to generate your own test data. You can also simulate a number of scenarios for testing in Sandbox. Some of the most common Sandbox scenarios are listed below. For additional product-specific testing scenarios, see the documentation for the specific product you are using, or Test credentials.
47: Many of these scenarios can be run from Sandbox Studio without writing code, including per-product flows for Auth, Identity, Transactions, Investments, Liabilities, Assets, Statements, Signal, Transfer, and processor tokens.
48: ITEM_LOGIN_REQUIRED
49: Update mode in Link is used to handle user logins that have become invalid (for example, due to the user changing their password at their financial institution). An Item that needs to be handled via update mode will enter the ITEM_LOGIN_REQUIRED error state. To test your update mode flow in Sandbox, you can use the /sandbox/item/reset_login endpoint to force an Item into this state. Sandbox Items will also automatically enter the ITEM_LOGIN_REQUIRED state 30 days after being created.
50: An example of using update mode and testing in Sandbox can be found in the Plaid Pattern sample app. Items.js illustrates how to incorporate the handling and testing of update mode using the /sandbox/item/reset_login endpoint.
51: Consent expiration
52: Some institutions enforce an expiration date on Item consent, after which the Item stops returning data until the user renews consent via update mode. To test this, create an Item at First Platypus Bank - OAuth (ins_129644), First Platypus Bank - OAuth App2App (ins_132241), or Flexible Platypus Open Banking (ins_117181), test institutions that populate consent_expiration_time. Items created at these institutions are assigned a consent_expiration_time 30 days from the time the Item is created.
53: Instant Match and micro-deposit-based Auth
54: While the standard Instant Auth flow does not require special configuration to test, the additional Auth flows such as Instant Match, Same-Day Micro-deposits, and Automated micro-deposits require more complex steps such as verifying micro-deposits or routing numbers. The Sandbox environment provides several test institutions and endpoints that can be used to verify these flows. For more details, see Testing Auth flows.
55: Returning user experience
56: The Link returning user experience (formerly known as Remember Me) can be tested in Sandbox using Sandbox Profiles, which represent users who have connected accounts to Plaid before. More details can be found at Testing Plaid accounts in Sandbox.
57: Transactions updates
58: To simulate updating transactions, see Testing pending and posted transactions.
59: Webhooks
60: Plaid provides a special Sandbox-only endpoint, /sandbox/item/fire_webhook, that can be used to trigger a number of webhooks on demand, allowing you to test that you are receiving webhooks successfully. Certain products, and webhooks that are associated with a user rather than an Item, have their own Sandbox webhook endpoints; for the full list, see the Sandbox API reference.
61: All webhooks that would be fired in Production will also fire in Sandbox, except when using the Transfer product, and except for Investments DEFAULT_UPDATE webhooks, which typically do not fire in Sandbox due to the lack of dynamic holdings and investment transactions data.
62: Sandbox MCP server
63: Plaid has a Sandbox MCP server,
64: which, when run locally, allows your AI-powered agent to work with the Sandbox directly. Your agent can
65: fire webhooks, create a Sandbox Item and access token without going through Link,
66: generate mock user data, and search the Plaid documentation.
67: Testing with live data using a Trial plan
68: Free Trial plans (US and Canada only) are available to new Plaid teams created on or after April 15, 2026.
69: Using a Trial plan, you can test many Plaid products with real production data for free.
70: When using a Trial plan, be sure to persist your access tokens and do not lose track of them. All access tokens created in Production will count against your Trial plan Item limit.
71: For more details on Trial plans, see Billing: Trial plans.
72: Differences between Sandbox and Production
73: Aside from the fact that Sandbox uses test data and has special endpoints that can be used, Sandbox has the following special attributes:
74: Does not always reflect institution-specific behaviors and quirks. For example, Sandbox does not reflect institution-specific transaction history limits, and institutions that do not return pending transactions in Production may return pending transactions in Sandbox. Similarly, all Sandbox OAuth institutions use a single generic OAuth flow rather than institution-specific OAuth behavior. Certain institution-specific behaviors may be tested using Sandbox test institutions.
75: Does not send emails or text messages, such as confirmation emails after a user has linked an account, or text message reminders for the micro-deposit flow.
76: Does not require a use case to be set, even if you are enrolled in Data Transparency Messaging.
77: Allows http for redirect URIs, while Production requires https.
78: Does not perform any OCR or image processing. To test flows that require these, such as Identity Verification Selfie Checks or Document Income, see the testing section for the specific product you are testing.
79: Sandbox data is not always based on a consistent data source across different API calls, especially across different products. For example, Sandbox transaction history may show income and outflow inconsistent with the balance shown on the account, and some products, like Signal, generate random results in Sandbox. Triggering a transfer using a Transfer endpoint will not cause that transaction to show up when calling /transactions/sync or change the balance of the account when calling /accounts/balance/get. Sandbox Profiles and custom test data give you a consistent data source across products when you need one.
80: Sandbox may not show the latest updates to the Link UI until those updates have been rolled out to all eligible customers. This may occasionally result in temporary discrepancies between the Sandbox Link UI and the Production Link UI.
81: In the OAuth flow, Sandbox will not enforce the checkboxes for "Select additional information you want to share" and will behave as though all boxes in that section are checked.
82: Returning user profiles are scoped to your Plaid team, unlike in Production, where returning user recognition is global to Plaid. Two teams using the same phone number will get two independent profiles.
83: Returning users are recognized by phone number only. Unlike in Production, user.email_address is not used to find a returning user's Plaid account.
84: Seeded profiles carry trusted-device state that is visible through the API, but it is not matched against a real browser's device fingerprint, so saved accounts will still prompt for authentication. In Production, trusted device state is matched against the user's actual device.
85: Returning user and Layer authentication only supports OTP, using the code 123456; Silent Network Authentication and mobile carrier checks are not run. In Production, authentication is dynamic and includes SNA and carrier checks.
86: For the Consumer Report product, Sandbox will not de-dupe duplicate accounts associated with the same user during report creation, unlike in Production.
87: One exception to the rule that Sandbox does not use real data is Monitor. While Identity Verification checks cannot be made against real databases in Sandbox, Sandbox does use real Monitor watchlists, although they may not be as up-to-date as the watchlists used in Production.
88: Testing with live data using Limited Production (deprecated)
89: Limited Production has been replaced with Trial plans for all Plaid teams created on or after April 15, 2026. Trial plans offer free access to the Plaid API and, unlike Limited Production, provide access to almost all institutions prior to full Production approval.
90: To use Link with bank data in Production or Limited Production in the US or Canada, all customers who created accounts after October 31, 2024 must select a use case description from the Customize > Link section of the Dashboard.
91: Prior to obtaining Production access, you can make free API calls using live data in Limited Production.
92: You can request Limited Production access via the Dashboard, either by clicking the "Test with Real Data" link on the Dashboard homepage, or by going directly to the Limited Production request form.
93: In Limited Production, the following restrictions apply:
94: There is a cap on the number of API calls you can make for each product. Both failed and successful API calls count against this cap. API calls that do not relate to a specific product (such as /accounts/get) do not count against this cap.
95: There is a cap on the total number of Items you can create, unless you have full Production access for at least one product.
96: You cannot access certain major financial institutions, including Bank of America, Chase, and Wells Fargo, unless you have full Production access for at least one product and have also completed the OAuth registration process.
97: The following products are supported in Limited Production: Assets, Auth, Balance, Identity (including Identity Match), Income, Investments, Liabilities, Payment Initiation, Transactions (including Transactions Refresh and Recurring Transactions), and Enrich. To test other products with live data, request Production access.
98: If testing Payment Initiation in Limited Production, limitations on the type and quantity of payments apply. For details, see Testing Payment Initiation.
99: To remove the limits on your Limited Production access, apply for full Production access. Once you have full Production access for a product, usage limits for that product will be removed from your account. If you have any free API calls remaining, as long as you are a direct customer of Plaid, you can continue to use them after receiving Production access; once those credits have been used up, your usage will be billed as normal Production traffic. If you are not a direct customer of Plaid and instead are accessing Plaid via a reseller partner, your free API credits will expire once you receive full Production access.
100: If you add a subscription-billed product to an Item in Limited Production (for example, by creating an Item initialized with Transactions, Investments, or Liabilities), you will not be charged for that subscription unless you continue to use the Item after using up your free API requests and receiving full Production access.
101: If you require additional API calls in Limited Production to evaluate a product, file a support ticket.
102: Developer community
103: GitHub
104: YouTube
105: Discord

33: Plaid pricing and billing
34: Learn about pricing, what is considered a billable event, and how to monitor your bill
35: Pricing information
36: To view pricing, apply for Production access. Detailed pricing for Pay-as-you-go and Growth plans appears before you submit your request. To learn more about Custom pricing, contact sales.
37: Pricing plans
38: Plaid offers four pricing plans:
39: Trial – Best for exploring Plaid or building a hobby project. Free access, with a limit of 10 Production Items. To learn more, see Trial plans.
40: Pay-as-you-go – Best for individuals and solo developers. No minimum spend, commitment, or usage cap. You pay each month for what you use. Includes Plaid's core products and self-service support via docs, help center, and community resources.
41: Growth – Best for startups and new businesses. Annual plan with a minimum spend commitment and discounted rates. Includes business-focused features such as support with response-time SLAs (service-level agreements), single sign-on (SSO), and a dedicated account manager for qualifying contracts.
42: Custom (also called Scale) – Best for businesses that need flexible billing or support for regulated industries. Offers the lowest rates, with custom commitments and billing terms. Includes every Plaid product and access to beta products. Integration assistance and premium support are available as add-ons.
43: To sign up for a Trial or Pay-as-you-go plan, use the Dashboard. For a Growth or Custom plan, or if you're not sure which plan is right for you, contact sales. To change your plan later, see Viewing or changing pricing plans.
44: Plan and product availability
45: EU and UK customers
46: If your business is based in the EU or UK, or serves end users there, only Custom plans are available.
47: Core products available on all paid plans
48: Auth
49: Balance
50: Identity
51: Identity Match
52: Investments Move
53: Assets
54: Income
55: Statements
56: Enrich
57: Investments
