FIX Market Data (MD) 49: | Mode | Production | Testnet | 50: | ---------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- | 51: | Standard | `tcp+tls://fix-md.binance.com:9000` | `tcp+tls://fix-md.testnet.binance.vision:9000` | 52: | FIX request / FIX SBE response | `tcp+tls://fix-md.binance.com:9001` | `tcp+tls://fix-md.testnet.binance.vision:9001` | 53: | FIX SBE request / FIX SBE response | `tcp+tls://fix-md.binance.com:9002` | `tcp+tls://fix-md.testnet.binance.vision:9002` | 54: 55: ## Can I use the `/sapi` endpoints on the Spot Test Network? 56: No, only the `/api` endpoints are available on the Spot Test Network: 57: - [Market Data Endpoints (REST API)](rest-api.md#market-data-endpoints) 58: - [Market Data Requests (WebSocket API)](web-socket-api.md#market-data-requests) 59: - [WebSocket Market Streams](web-socket-streams.md) 60: - [Trading Endpoints (REST API)](rest-api.md#trading-endpoints) 61: - [Account Endpoints (REST API)](rest-api.md#account-endpoints) 62: - [Trading Requests (WebSocket API)](web-socket-api.md#trading-requests) 63: - [Account Requests (WebSocket API)](web-socket-api.md#account-requests) 64: - [User Data Streams](user-data-stream.md) 65: 66: ## How to get funds in/out of the Spot Test Network? 67: All users registering on the Spot Test Network automatically receive a balance in many different 68: assets. Please note that these are not real assets and can be used only on the Spot Test Network 69: itself. 70: All funds on the Spot Test Network are virtual, and can not be transferred in/out of the Spot Test 71: Network. 72: 73: ## What are the restrictions on the Spot Test Network? 74: **IP Limits**, **Order Rate Limits**, **Exchange Filters** and **Symbol Filters** on the Spot Test 75: Network are generally the same as on the Spot API. 76: All users are encouraged to regularly query the API to get the most up-to-date rate limits & 77: filters, for example by doing: 78: ``` 79: curl "https://testnet.binance.vision/api/v3/exchangeInfo" 80: ``` 81: 82: ## All my data has disappeared! What happened? 83: The Spot Test Network is periodically reset to a blank state. That includes all pending and executed 84: orders. During that reset procedure, all users automatically receive a fresh allowance of all 85: assets. 86: These resets happen approximately **once per month**, and we do not offer prior notification for 87: them. 88: Starting from August 2020, API Keys are preserved during resets. Users no longer need to re-register 89: new API Keys after a reset. 90: 91: ## What is the difference between `klines` and `uiKlines`? 92: On the Spot Test Network, these 2 requests always return the same data. 93: 94: ## What are RSA API Keys? 95: RSA API Keys are an alternative to the typical HMAC-SHA-256 API Keys that are used to authenticate 96: your requests on the Spot API. 97: Unlike HMAC-SHA-256 API Keys where we generate the secret signing key for you, with RSA API Keys, 98: _you_ generate a pair of public+private RSA keys, send us the public key, and sign your requests 99: with your private key. 100: 101: ## What type of RSA keys are supported? 102: We support RSA keys of any length from 2048 bits up to 4096 bits. We recommend **2048 bits keys** as 103: a good balance between security and signature speed. 104: When generating the RSA signature, use the **PKCS#1 v1.5** signature scheme. This is the default 105: when using OpenSSL. We currently do not support the PSS signature scheme. 106: 107: ## How can I use RSA API Keys? 108: Step 1: Generate the private key `test-prv-key.pem`. **Do not share this file with anyone!** 109: ``` 110: openssl genrsa -out test-prv-key.pem 2048 111: ``` 112: Step 2: Generate the public key `test-pub-key.pem` from the private key. 113: ``` 114: openssl rsa -in test-prv-key.pem -pubout -outform PEM -out test-pub-key.pem 115: ``` 116: The public key should look something like this: 117: ``` 118: -----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY----- 119: bL4DUXwR3ijFSXzcecQtVFU1zVWcSQd0Meztl3DLX42l/8EALJx3LSz9YKS0PMQW 120: MIICIjANBgkqhkiG9w0BAQEFAAOCAg8AMIICCgKCAgEAv9ij99RAJM4JLl8Rg47b 121: dJXMrv84WL1OK/gid4hCnxo083LYLXUpIqMmL+O6fmXAvsvkyMyT520Cw0ZNCrUk 122: WoCjGE4JZZGF4wOkWdF37JFWbDnE/GF5mAykKj+OMaECBlZ207KleQqgVzHjKuCb 123: hPMuBVVD3IhjBfIc7EEM438LbtayMDx4dviPWwm127jwn8qd9H3kv5JBoDfsdYMB 124: 3k39r724CljqlAfX33GpbV2LvEkL6Da3OFk+grfN98X2pCBRz5+1N95I2cRD7o+j 125: wtCr+65E+Gqjo4OI60F9Gq5GDcrnudnUw13a4zwlU6W+Cy8gJ4R0CcKTc4+VhYVX 126: 5wW2tzLVnDqvjIN8hjhgtmUv8hr19Wn+42ev+5sNtO5QAS6sJMJG5D+cpxCNhei1 127: Xm+1zXliaA1fvVYRqon2MdHcedFeAjzVtX38+Xweytowydcq2V/9pUUNZIzUqX7t 128: Zr3F+Ao3QOb/CuWbUBpUcbXfGv7AI1ozP8LRByyu6O8Z1dZNdkdjWVt83maUrIJH 129: jjc7jlZY9JbH6EyYV5TenjJaupvdlx72vA7Fcgevx87seog2JALAJqZQNT+t9/tm 130: rTUSEp3t4aINKUC1QC0CYKECAwEAAQ== 131: -----END PUBLIC KEY----- 132: ``` 133: Step 3: Register your public key on the Spot Test Network. 134: During registration, we will generate an API Key for you that you will have to put in the 135: `X-MBX-APIKEY` header of your requests, exactly the same way as you would do for HMAC-SHA-256 API 136: Keys. 137: Step 4: When you send a request to the Spot Test Network, sign the payload using your private key. 138: Here is an example Bash script to post a new order and sign the request using OpenSSL. You can adapt 139: it to your favorite programming language: 140: ```bash 141: #!/usr/bin/env bash 142: # Set up authentication: 143: API_KEY="put your own API Key here" 144: PRIVATE_KEY_PATH="test-prv-key.pem" 145: # Set up the request: 146: API_METHOD="POST" 147: API_CALL="api/v3/order" 148: API_PARAMS="symbol=BTCUSDT&side=SELL&type=LIMIT&timeInForce=GTC&quantity=1&price=0.2" 149: # Sign the request: 150: timestamp=$(date +%s000) 151: api_params_with_timestamp="$API_PARAMS×tamp=$timestamp" 152: signature=$(echo -n "$api_params_with_timestamp" \ 153: | openssl dgst -sha256 -sign "$PRIVATE_KEY_PATH" \ 154: | openssl enc -base64 -A) 155: # Send the request: 156: curl -H "X-MBX-APIKEY: $API_KEY" -X "$API_METHOD" \ 157: "https://testnet.binance.vision/$API_CALL?$api_params_with_timestamp" \ 158: --data-urlencode "signature=$signature" 159: ``` 160: 161: ## What are Ed25519 API keys? 162: Ed25519 API keys are an alternative to [RSA API keys](#what-are-rsa-api-keys), using asymmetric 163: cryptography to authenticate your requests on the Spot API. 164: Like RSA API keys, Ed25519 keys are _asymmetric_: you generate a keypair, share the public key with 165: Binance, and use your private key to sign requests. 166: 167: ## Why use Ed25519 instead of RSA API keys? 168: Ed25519 digital signature scheme provides security comparable to 3072-bit RSA keys, while having 169: much smaller signatures that are faster to compute: 170: | API key type | Signature size | Signature operation | 171: | -------------- | -------------- | ------------------- | 172: | HMAC-SHA-256 | 64 bytes | 0.00 ms | 173: | Ed25519 | 88 bytes | 0.03 ms | 174: | RSA (2048-bit) | 344 bytes | 0.55 ms | 175: | RSA (4096-bit) | 684 bytes | 3.42 ms | 176: 177: ## How can I use Ed25519 API keys? 178: Step 1: Generate the private key `test-prv-key.pem`. **Do not share this file with anyone!** 179: ``` 180: openssl genpkey -algorithm ed25519 -out test-prv-key.pem 181: ``` 182: Step 2: Compute the public key `test-pub-key.pem` from the private key. 183: ``` 184: openssl pkey -pubout -in test-prv-key.pem -out test-pub-key.pem 185: ``` 186: The public key should look something like this: 187: ``` 188: -----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY----- 189: MCowBQYDK2VwAyEACeCSz7VJkh3Bb+NF794hLMU8fLB9Zr+/tGMdVKCC2eo= 190: -----END PUBLIC KEY----- 191: ``` 192: Step 3: Register your public key on the Spot Test Network. 193: During registration, we will generate an API key for you. Please put it in the `X-MBX-APIKEY` header 194: of your requests, exactly the same way as with other API key types. 195: Step 4: When you send a request to the Spot Test Network, sign the payload using your private key. 196: Here is an example in Python that posts a new order signed with Ed25519 key. You can adapt it to 197: your favorite programming language. 198: ```python 199: #!/usr/bin/env python3 200: import base64 201: import requests 202: import time 203: from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.serialization import load_pem_private_key 204: # Set up authentication 205: API_KEY='put your own API Key here' 206: PRIVATE_KEY_PATH='test-prv-key.pem' 207: # Load the private key. 208: # In this example the key is expected to be stored without encryption, 209: # but we recommend using a strong password for improved security. 210: with open(PRIVATE_KEY_PATH, 'rb') as f: 211: private_key = load_pem_private_key(data=f.read(), 212: password=None) 213: # Set up the request parameters 214: params = { 215: 'symbol': 'BTCUSDT', 216: 'side': 'SELL', 217: 'type': 'LIMIT', 218: 'timeInForce': 'GTC', 219: 'quantity': '1.0000000', 220: 'price': '0.20', 221: } 222: # Timestamp the request 223: timestamp = int(time.time() * 1000) # UNIX timestamp in milliseconds 224: params['timestamp'] = timestamp 225: # Sign the request 226: payload = '&'.join([f'{param}={value}' for param, value in params.items()]) 227: signature = base64.b64encode(private_key.sign(payload.encode('ASCII'))) 228: params['signature'] = signature 229: # Send the request 230: headers = { 231: 'X-MBX-APIKEY': API_KEY, 232: } 233: response = requests.post( 234: 'https://testnet.binance.vision/api/v3/order', 235: headers=headers, 236: data=params, 237: ) 238: print(response.json()) 239: ```

1: Note
2: Note about deprecation of TLS1.0 and TLS1.1
3: As we mentioned in our previous blog posts, we’re no longer supporting TLS1.0 and TLS1.1 starting June 1st, 2022. We’ll only support TLS1.2 or higher going forward. Refer to our blog for more details:
4: TLS 1.0 and 1.1 Disablement for the Intuit Developer Group
5: Upgrading your apps to support TLS 1.2
6: Set up OAuth 2.0
7: Use the OAuth 2.0 protocol to implement authentication and authorization. Authorization is essential for both testing via sandbox companies and production apps.
8: We’ll show you how to set up the authorization flow so users can authorize to your app and give it permission to connect to their QuickBooks Online company.
9: If users grant permission, our Intuit OAuth 2.0 Server sends an authorization code back to your app. Your app exchanges this code for access tokens. These tokens are tied to your users’ now authorized QuickBooks Online company (identified by the realmID).
10: Your app needs access tokens to make API calls and interact with QuickBooks Online data.
11: Step 1: Create your app on the Intuit Developer Portal
12: Start by signing in to your developer account and creating an app on the Intuit Developer Portal.
13: When you create your app, select the QuickBooks Online Accounting scope.
14: This app provides the credentials you’ll need for authorization requests.
15: Step 2: Practice authorization in the OAuth Playground
16: Check out the OAuth Playground to preview each step of the authorization flow. We’ve provided sample data, like the redirect URI, so you can focus on the overall flow.
17: Using the OAuth Playground isn’t required, but we recommend it.
18: Step 3: Start developing with an SDK
19: Our SDKs come with a built-in OAuth 2.0 Client Library and handle many parts of the authorization implementation for you. For instance, our SDKs implement handlers that automatically exchange the authorization codes sent from the Intuit OAuth 2.0 Server for access tokens.
20: Select a link to download an SDK:
21: OAuth 2.0 Client Library for .Net
22: OAuth 2.0 Client Library for Java
23: OAuth 2.0 Client Library for PHP
24: OAuth 2.0 Client Library for Node.js
25: OAuth 2.0 Client Library for Python
26: OAuth 2.0 Client Library for Ruby
27: .NET
28: Java
29: PHP
30: Node.js
31: Python
32: Ruby

38: Download the latest version of oauth2-platform-api.jar and include it in your project.
39: Sample below shows how to add it to a gradle project:
40: compile (group: 'com.intuit.quickbooks-online', name: 'oauth2-platform-api', version: '6.0.7', classifier: 'jar-with-dependencies')

49: Note: Our SDKs are only for OAuth 2.0 and QuickBooks Online. SDKs aren’t required to develop an awesome app. However, given the importance of OAuth implementation, we strongly encourage you use them.
50: Step 4: Understand the end-to-end authorization flow
51: While authorization is a simple step for app users, it involves several tasks on the backend. Here’s an brief overview:
52: Creating authorization requests
53: Review the scopes you selected for your app. These determine what data and API it can access. You may want to use the openID scope to implement OpenID Connect in addition to others.
54: Configure your app so it uses the correct credentials (i.e., Client ID and Client secret) and redirect URIs.
55: Review the base URLs in our authorization discovery documents.
56: Use this info to create authorization requests.
57: Managing the authorization flow
58: When a user connects to your app, it sends an authorization request to the Intuit OAuth 2.0 Server.
59: The user gets redirected to an authorization page where they can give your app permission to access their QuickBooks Online company and its data. This is the “user consent” step of the process.
60: If the user authorizes your app, the Intuit OAuth 2.0 Server sends an authorization code back to your app.
61: Getting access and refresh tokens
62: Your app sends the authorization code back to the Intuit OAuth 2.0 Server and exchanges it for access and refresh tokens.
63: Your app extracts the latest access and refresh tokens from the server response.
64: Making API calls
65: Use access tokens to call specific APIs and interact with users’ QuickBooks Online company data.
66: When access tokens expire, use a refresh token to “refresh” the access token.
67: If a refresh token expires, users need to go through the authorization flow again.
68: Step 5: Get your app’s credentials
69: Sign in to your Intuit Developer account and get your app’s Client ID and Client secret.
70: If you’re implementing authorization for a live, in-production app, go to the Production section and select Keys & OAuth to get your credentials.
71: If you’re implementing authorization for testing with a sandbox company, go to the Development section and select Keys & OAuth to get your credentials.
72: Step 6: Learn about discovery documents
73: OAuth 2.0 requires multiple URLs for authentication and requests for resources like tokens, user info, and credentials.
74: Use our discovery documents to simplify the implementation. These JSON documents, found at a well known location, contain field : value pairs and URL endpoints for authorization, token, userinfo, and other data points.
75: Step 7: Add your app’s redirect URIs
76: URIs handle responses from the Intuit OAuth 2.0 Server during the authorization flow. Basically, they’re your app’s endpoints.
77: Add at least one redirect URI for your app.
78: If you’re developing with an SDK, use the URI value generated by the SDK.
79: Tip: As a best practice, design your app’s endpoints so they don’t expose authorization codes to other resources on the page. Learn more about URIs and OAuth 2.0.
80: Step 8: Create an authorization request
81: Create the authorization request your app will send to the Intuit OAuth 2.0 Server when users connect to your app.
82: Authorization request parameters
83: Request parameters should identify your app and include the required scopes.
84: Field
85: Description
86: Required
87: client_id
88: Identifies the app making the request. You got the client_id value in Step 5.
89: Yes
90: scope
91: Lists the scopes your app uses.
92: Enter one or more scopes. The list should be space-delimited. The scope value defines the type of data an app can utilize. This information appears on the authorization page users see when they connect to your app.
93: Tip: We recommend apps request scopes incrementally based on your feature requirements, rather than all scopes up front.
94: Yes
95: redirect_uri
96: Determines where the Intuit OAuth 2.0 Server redirects users to if they authorize your app. The redirect value must match the URI you listed in Step 7, including casing, http scheme, and trailing “/.”
97: Yes
98: response_type
99: States if the Intuit OAuth 2.0 endpoint returns an authorization code.
100: Always set the value to “code”. Example: ``code_type``= code
101: Yes
102: state
103: Defines the state between your authorization request and the Intuit OAuth 2.0 Server response.
104: The state field is used for validation. It checks if the client (i.e., your app) gets the data back that it sent in the original request. Meaning, the state is maintained from send to response.
105: You can enter any string value for the state. The server should return the exact state : value pair sent in the original request.
106: Tip: We strongly recommend you include an anti-forgery token for the state and confirm it in the response. This prevents cross-site request forgery. Learn more about CSRF.
107: Yes
108: claims
109: Optional. A JSON Object containing a set of user claims that your application is requesting via OpenID Connect. These claims are either returned in the OpenID Connect ID token, or UserInfo response. Available claims include:
110: realmId —The realm ID of the specific QuickBooks company to which the user is associated. This claim is only populated if the user is currently logged into QuickBooks.

314: Step 10: Create the UI that redirects users to the authorization page
315: There are a few ways users can connect to your app:
316: Add a “Connect to” button somewhere in your app. When users select it, your app should redirect them and start the authorization flow. Here’s a quick guide to creating button UI.
317: If you list your app in the QuickBooks App Store, there are a few options. You can simply link to your app’s website where users can get your app. You can also set up Intuit Single Sign-on so users can connect to your app directly from your app page.
318: Since designing this UI may come later in development, we won’t focus on it here. However you decide to set up the UI, it needs to redirect users to the Intuit OAuth 2.0 Server and open the authorization page.
319: Preview the authorization page
320: This authorization page is where users authorize your app and give it permission to access their data. They’ll see your app’s name and the QuickBooks Online company they’re connecting with.
321: If they authorize your app, the server will redirect them back to the redirect URI you set.
322: Step 11: Get the authorization code from server response
323: At this point, your app is waiting for a response from the Intuit OAuth 2.0 Server.
324: If users authorize your app, the Intuit OAuth 2.0 Server sends a response to the redirect URI you specified in Step 7. The response contains an authorization code in the code field.
325: Copy the code value.
326: See an example server response for authorization codes
327: 1
328: 2
329: 3
330: 4
331: https://www.mydemoapp.com/oauth-redirect?
332: code=4/P7q7W91a-oMsCeLvIaQm6bTrgtp7&
333: state=security_token%3D138r5719ru3e1%26url%3Dhttps://www.mydemoapp.com/oauth-redirect&
334: realmId=1231434565226279
335: Parameter
336: Description
337: code
338: The authorization code sent by the Intuit OAuth 2.0 Server.
339: Max length: 512 characters
340: realmId
341: The unique ID of the connected user’s QuickBooks Online company. It’s also sometimes called the “company ID.- Use the realmId for subsequent API endpoint URLs to get data from QuickBooks Online companies.
342: state
343: The state value sent from the Intuit OAuth 2.0 Server. It should match the state sent in the original authorization request.
344: If users don’t authorize your app, the server sends an access_denied error.
345: If the authorization request has a scope issue, the server sends an invalid_scope error.
346: Note: If your response endpoint renders an HTML page, other resources on that page can see the authorization code in the URL. Scripts can read the URL directly, and all resources may be sent to the URL in the caller and Referer HTTP header. Carefully consider if you want to send authorization credentials this way. This is especially important for third-party scripts, such as social plugins and analytics. To avoid issues, we recommend the server first handle the request, then redirect to another URL that doesn’t include the response parameters.

1: Publish your app
2: Publish your app and put it into production. This makes it live and functional. You can share the URL of the app with users so they can access it.
3: Follow these steps to get production credentials. Use them in your code to make your app live and ready to use.
4: If you want to make your app publicly available, here’s how to list your app on the QuickBooks App Store.
5: Step 1: Fill out the App Details for Production
6: Sign in to your developer account.
7: Select My Hub > App dashboard from the upper-right corner of the toolbar.
8: Select and open the app you want to publish.
9: Select Keys and credentials from the left navigation pane.
10: Select Production.
11: Select App Details and fill in all the details.
12: Select the down arrow of the first section and fill in your email address and other details.
13: In the next section, enter the URLs for your End User License Agreement and Privacy Policy.
14: In the next, add your app’s host domain, launch URL, disconnect URL, and connect/reconnect URL.
15: In the next, select up to four categories for your app. These help your users understand what your app does.
16: In the next, check any regulated industries that you built the app for.
17: Select the regions where your app is hosted.
18: This should take about 30 minutes to complete.
19: Step 2: Review OAuth 2.0
20: Make sure you’ve fully set up OAuth 2.0 for your app.
21: Before you go live, try connecting, disconnecting, and reconnecting your app from a sandbox company. This helps catch and prevent errors in your OAuth2.0 setup.
22: Step 3: Update your Intuit Developer Account profile
23: Sign in to your developer account.
24: Select My Hub > Account Profile from the upper-right corner of the toolbar.
25: Review your contact and account info.
26: Step 4: Complete the App Assessment Questionnaire
27: Sign in to your developer account.
28: Select My Hub > Account Profile from the upper-right corner of the toolbar.
29: Select and open the app you want to publish.
30: Go to Keys and credentials from the left navigation pane.
31: Select Production and then select Compliance.
32: Select Start Questionnaire.
33: Complete the questionnaire.
34: These URLs are required before you can get your production credentials.
35: Step 5: Review your app’s name, icon, and other settings
36: With the app still open on your developer account:
37: Review the naming and logo guidelines for published apps.
38: Sign in to your developer account.
39: Select and open the app you want to publish.
40: Select Settings from the left navigation pane.
41: Select the Basic app info tab and review the app name and the icon. Upload the image you want users to see when they download your app.
42: Check the rest of the tabs to ensure that all information is correct.
43: Step 6: Get your app’s production credentials
44: Now you have all the correct info and settings in place. It’s time to get your app’s Client ID and Client Secret so you can code it into your app and make calls to our API.
45: Sign in to your developer account.
46: Select and open the app you want to publish.
47: Select Keys and credentials from the left navigation pane.
48: Select Production and turn on Show Credentials. Note: The Show Credentials switch appears only after the App Assessment Questionnaire is approved.
49: Copy the Client ID and Client secret.
50: Use these credentials for your production app. Put them into relevant variables and settings in your code. This givesy our app access QuickBooks Online data and our API.
51: You can share the URL with other developers or users so they can access your app, keeping it semi-private.
52: Next steps: List on the QuickBooks App Store
53: If you want to use your app privately, it’s now live and functional.
54: Want to make your app publicly available to millions of QuickBooks Online users? Here’s how to list your app on the QuickBooks App Store.

1: Build with Intuit Developer Plugin
2: Use Intuit Developer Plugin to set up your developer workspace, create an app, configure scopes, authenticate, and make your first QuickBooks API call from an AI-enabled development environment.
3: Intuit Developer Plugin helps you complete the setup steps required to call Intuit APIs without switching between the Developer Portal, API docs, OAuth guides, and your IDE.
4: What is Intuit Developer Plugin?
5: Intuit Developer Plugin is an AI-assisted onboarding experience for developers building with Intuit APIs.
6: It guides you through the setup flow for your first API call:
7: Intuit Developer Plugin is designed for developer setup and API onboarding.
8: Who should use this guide?

10: New to Intuit Developer and want to make your first QuickBooks API call

15: Before you begin

17: An Intuit Developer account
18: Access to a developer workspace
19: A clear first API goal, such as listing invoices, retrieving company information, or testing a basic sandbox request
20: Use sandbox data while building and testing.
21: Do not use production credentials or production company data for initial setup.
22: Security best practices

24: Use sandbox while building and testing
25: Use least-privilege scopes
26: Review any scope change before approving it

28: Do not paste secrets into AI prompts or public tools

30: Rotate credentials if they are exposed
31: Review generated requests and code before using them

28: Remote MCP
29: Can I connect to more than one organisation?
30: Yes. A user can authorise several organisations for the same app. Ask the agent to list the connected organisations, then tell it which one to act on. Each organisation still goes through the standard OAuth consent step.
31: Can I see what my agent did?
32: Every Xero API call your agent makes is logged in the Developer Portal, under the app you own. Only the API calls are logged, not the tool calls or prompts behind them. If you need a record of what your agent asked for and why, you will need to log that in your own client or agent.
33: Can I try it before I upgrade?
34: Yes, apps on Starter plan can use it with the demo organisation. You can connect, run the tools, and decide whether it's worth upgrading to Core. Real customer organisations need the Core plan or above.
35: Can I use a web app instead of PKCE?
36: Technically yes. We don't recommend it. A web app's client ID and client secret are easy to paste into an AI-enabled tool by accident, and a PKCE app removes that risk.
37: Can I use the Remote MCP for free as an Accountant or Bookkeeper?
38: Yes. If you’re building an integration for your practice or a client, MCP access is included in your API fee exemption. To apply, go to Manage plan for your app in the Developer Portal and select Get in touch.
39: Do I need a Custom Connection?
40: No. Custom Connections apps are not eligible to access the Remote MCP Server.
41: Does a tool call run against one organisation or several?
42: One. Each call runs against a single organisation.
43: Does certification apply?
44: Certification rules haven't changed. Apps on Plus, Advanced and Enterprise must be certified, whether or not they use Remote MCP.
45: Does my client need to support OAuth?
46: Yes. The server authorises through Xero's OAuth 2.0 flow with PKCE, so your client needs to be able to start that flow.
47: Does the server ask the user to confirm before changing Xero data?
48: The tools on V1 do not elicit user confirmation. Always ask your agent to confirm with you before writing anything back to Xero.
49: How do I disconnect an organisation or revoke access?
50: The user who authorized can disconnect access from their Connected Apps page in the Xero App.
51: The app developer can manage connections through the Connection Management page in the Developer Portal. See Managing Connections.
52: How is this different from the Xero connector in Claude?
53: The Developer Remote MCP is for developers & builders building custom agents and apps. It can be used with any MCP compatible client and offers tools that reads and writes Xero data. It supports multiple organisations with user consent.
54: What are the rate limits?
55: Rate limits are the same as Xero APIs. Today that's 1,000 calls per day per organisation on the Starter plan and 5,000 per day per organisation on the Core plan and above, per the pricing page.
56: What model should I use?
57: Use a model with sufficient reasoning you trust for your financial data.
58: What scopes does it need?
59: Only the scopes for the tools you want the agent to call. Each tool's required scope is listed in the tools table.
60: What should my agent do to avoid writing to the wrong organisation?
61: Always ask your agent to confirm with you before writing anything back to Xero. The server doesn't do this for you. For development, point the agent at the demo organisation and say that in its instructions.
62: What tools are available?
63: The full tool list with scopes is in the documentation.
64: What's the server URL?
65: https://api.xero.com/mcp/v1
66: Which MCP clients does it work with?
67: Any client that supports remote MCP servers. We've documented setup for Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor and VS Code.
68: Who can use it?
69: The Remote MCP is included on plans Core and above. Apps on the Starter plan can use it with the demo organisation only. See Xero Developer Pricing and Policies.
70: Why PKCE?
71: PKCE doesn't need a client secret, so there's no secret to leak into a prompt, a config file or an AI development tool.
72: Why would I use the official server instead of a community one?
73: It's built, monitored and maintained by the team that builds the API. It uses the same OAuth 2.0 sign-in, permissions and rate limits as the rest of the Xero API, and the layer between your AI tool and your accounting data runs on Xero infrastructure.

28: Custom Integration
29: 01. What's changing with Custom Connections?
30: From 1 December 2026, we are making changes to Custom Connections. From that date, you won't be able to:
31: Create a new Custom Connection app
32: Buy a new Custom Connection subscription
33: 02. What can I do before 1 December 2026?
34: Until 1 December 2026, you can create Custom Connection apps, buy Custom Connection subscriptions, and add or cancel subscriptions for Custom Connections apps.
35: 03. What happens to my existing Custom Connection App after 1 December 2026?
36: A Custom Connection app created before 1 December 2026 continues working the way it does today, maintaining the same API access and daily call limit it has now.
37: 04. Will client credentials still be available for machine-to-machine integrations?
38: Yes. Client credentials isn’t going away. We know it’s the right model for many machine-to-machine integrations, and we’re keeping it as part of the Xero Developer platform. We’ll share more about how client credentials will be offered in future updates on developer.xero.com from 1 December 2026.
39: 05. I have an existing Custom Connection subscription that isn’t connected to an app. What happens?
40: You have until 15 February 2027 to connect your unused subscription to an app or cancel it.
41: Connect it: You can still connect unused subscriptions to an existing Custom Connection app until 15 February 2027. Steps to connect an unused subscription to an existing app can be found here.
42: Cancel it: You can cancel at any time before 16 February 2027. Steps to cancel unused subscriptions are found here.
43: Do nothing: On 16 February 2027, if you haven’t connected or canceled your unused subscriptions, we’ll cancel them for you, so you stop paying for something you’re not using.
44: Once a subscription is cancelled, it can’t be bought again.
45: 06. How do I manage my Custom Connection subscriptions?
46: You can manage this in Xero, by going to Settings > Connected apps > App Store subscriptions > Custom Connections. There you can manage your Custom Connection subscriptions or delete them, and update the payment method. Once a subscription is cancelled, it can’t be bought again.
47: 07. What happens if I delete a Custom Connection?
48: Until December 1 2026, you can delete a Custom Connection and create a new one. From 1 December 2026, a deleted Custom Connection can't be created again.
49: 08. Can a custom connection be connected to multiple organisations?
50: No, it can only be connected to a single organisation.
51: 09. Can an organisation have multiple custom connections?
52: Yes, organisations can purchase a Custom Connection for each app they’d like to connect. This won't affect the uncertified app limit. So an org can have 2 uncertified apps plus as many custom connection apps as needed.
53: 10. Can I access journals with a custom connection?
54: It depends on when you created your connection.
55: Connections created before 29 April 2026: These have broad scopes and can continue to access journals using the accounting.journals.read scope.
56: Connections created from 29 April 2026: these use new granular scopes, which don't include journal access.
57: 11. Can I make changes to a custom connection after it’s activated? Can I add more scopes or switch organisations?
58: Yes. If you choose to make changes to your custom connection it will be deactivated until it is re-authorised. You'll now use granular scopes for custom connections. More information is available here.
59: However, if you remove a broad scope from an existing connection, you won't be able to re-add it. Any broad scope you remove will be permanently replaced by granular scopes. You can continue to use your existing broad scopes until September 2027, as long as they remain in your configuration.
60: 12. Do access tokens expire?
61: Yes access tokens expire after 30 minutes but a new access token can be requested (as above) without user interaction.
62: 13. Do I need to manage refresh tokens?
63: No, refresh tokens are not required. An access token can be requested using only the client_id and client_secret.
64: 14. Do I need to specify the xero-tenant-id header when making API calls?
65: No, the xero-tenant-id header is not required. Each custom connection can only make calls against one organisation so only the access token is required.
66: 15. Do I need to write code to handle the authorisation flow?
67: No. When the developer creates a custom connection on developer.xero.com they will specify the email address of the authorising user (e.g. their client). That user will receive an email which guides them through the authorisation process.
68: If the developer is building an integration to an organization they have access to (e.g. for their own company) they can also be the authorising user.
69: 16. How can I test a Custom Connection?
70: Custom Connections can be tested using the demo company. There is no charge when using a demo company.
71: 17. How do I build a machine to machine integration?
72: If the organisation you're connecting to is in Australia, New Zealand, the UK or the US then you have the option of utilising our premium integration option Custom Connections.
73: If your organisation isn't in one of those regions, or you don't want to pay for a Custom Connection, then you can still make use of Web or PKCE code flow for building machine to machine integrations but you'll need to request your tokens and handle authorisation outside off your application.
74: 18. Will a Custom Connection require the use of scopes?
75: Yes. Scopes will be selected by the developer when a custom connection is created and displayed to the Xero user during authorisation. New custom connections will use the newly released granular scopes. More information is available here.
76: 19. Will you support long lived access tokens?
77: No, we've implemented short-lived tokens with long-lived authorizations as is best practice for OAuth 2.0. All Xero access tokens expire after 30 minutes. Refresh tokens allow your app to obtain new access tokens without involving a user again.
78: Alternatively, if you'd prefer not to have to manage a refresh token, you might be interested in the premium, Custom Connection option. It utilises the client credentials grant type and only requires your client id and client secret to request new access tokens.
79: 20. Will you support the client credentials grant type?
80: Yes, using the Client Credentials grant type provides an alternative way to retrieve information about your connections and users' subscriptions, without requiring the user's access or refresh tokens. You will however need a ClientID and a Client Secret.

40: To start making calls to Brex APIs, generate a user token from your Brex dashboard and pass it along in your API call headers.
41: 1. Generate a user token
42: Sign in to dashboard.brex.com as an account admin or card admin.
43: Go to Developer > Settings.
44: If your company has not accepted the developer API agreement, please review the terms and conditions. These must be accepted to use the developer API.
45: Click Create Token.
46: Create a name for your token that will help you identify it. Choose what level of data access you need for your application; these are the scopes your token will have.
47: The next screen will confirm your previous selections. Make sure it looks good, then select Allow Access.
48: Your token is now created. Copy and store the token securely. You won't be able to see it again.
49: Back on the developer page of your Brex dashboard, you should see your token listed now. As a security measure, part of the string is obfuscated. If you lose it, create a new one and replace the token.
50: Caution: Your user token is private and should not be shared. Never check it into version control or save it somewhere publicly accessible. If your user token is compromised or leaked, make sure to revoke it.
51: 2. Pass the user token in your API call headers
52: To pass your user token to Brex APIs, add it as a header to your API calls in the following format:
53: Authorization: "Bearer {{your user_token here}}"
54: If, for example, your user token value is bxt_jBWQLZXtu1f4sVT6UjaWPp7Gh9nVGjzEZgRX, your header will be:
55: Authorization: "Bearer bxt_jBWQLZXtu1f4sVT6UjaWPp7Gh9nVGjzEZgRX"
56: Token revocation and expiration
57: There are two scenarios where tokens will be invalid for authentication:
58: User tokens will expire if they are not used to make an API call for 90 days
59: User tokens associated to users in a non-active status will no longer work
60: If your token is compromised, or you no longer need it, revoke the user token from the developer page in your Brex dashboard. Once revoked, any calls made with this token will immediately begin to fail.
61: API Server
62: Brex currently only offers a production API server at https://api.brex.com. This is the base URL for all API calls.

40: Note: This section is only for Brex developer partners. If you are a Brex client–i.e., you have your own Brex account–looking to authenticate to our APIs, refer to the authentication page to get started.
41: API servers
42: Former API server URLs
43: As of January 1, 2026, we are transitioning base URLs to api.brex.com and api-staging.brex.com respectively, but the former URLs (platform.brexapis.com and platform.staging.brexapps.com) will continue to be available for the forseeable future.
44: Production: https://api.brex.com
45: Staging: https://api-staging.brex.com
46: Data in Staging
47: There are no availability guarantees in staging - data stored in staging environments may be purged at any time. Use staging for point-in-time testing only.
48: Scopes
49: openid: Required to make an OpenID Connect request.
50: offline_access: Required to obtain an OAuth 2.0 Refresh Token.
51: The scopes page describes how scopes work in the Brex API and the scopes required for each API.
52: Auth server
53: The base URL for the requests is:
54: Production: https://accounts-api.brex.com/oauth2/default
55: Staging: https://accounts-api.staging.brexapps.com/oauth2/default
56: OpenID Connect
57: The Brex API is fully compliant with OpenID Connect, an extension on top of OAuth 2.0. For more details on the OpenID Connect protocol, please see the spec. The well-known configuration can be found at the following URLs:
58: Production: https://accounts-api.brex.com/oauth2/default/.well-known/openid-configuration
59: Staging: https://accounts-api.staging.brexapps.com/oauth2/default/.well-known/openid-configuration
60: This may change in the future without notice. Always use the well-known OpenID configuration document as the source of truth for the base URL.
61: Authorization methods
62: Brex currently supports 2 different authorization grant types:
63: If you are using the onboarding API, you will generate a Client Credentials Grant as there is no existing Brex client involved.
64: For all other APIs, you will implement the Authorization Code Grant, which implements a web-based redirection flow to request permission from the Brex client to access their account. Only Brex clients with the proper roles may grant permission. Please see the User Roles & Permissions page for more details.
65: Authentication implementation
66: To implement authentication, we highly recommend using one of the existing OAuth 2.0 SDKs if available for your language. These SDKs handle the various intracies of the OAuth 2.0 spec and make it much easier to plug and play your credentials to get started.
67: Please contact our developer support team to be issued a client ID and client secret for partner authentication.
68: The prompt parameter
69: prompt is an optional parameter on the authorization request — the /v1/authorize URL you send the user to, not your redirect URI. It controls which screens a user sees when they already have a Brex session or an existing grant. Values are space-delimited, and Brex supports two of the values defined in 3.1.2.1. Authentication Request:
70: ValueEffect
71: loginAlways re-authenticate, even if the user has an active Brex session.
72: consentAlways show the consent screen, even if the user already granted every requested scope.
73: We recommend sending prompt=consent. The consent screen is where a user who can reach more than one Brex account chooses which account to connect; for example, an external firm like an accountant or bookkeeper can pick between the client accounts they operate on behalf of. Without forcing a selection, the OAuth authorization request would silently skip that screen and the user's primary account may be selected for them. See which account a token represents.
74: Send prompt=login when users of your application may have multiple Brex logins, to force re-authentication so they sign in as the login they mean to connect rather than whoever an active session belongs to. This is a separate concern from account selection: login decides which user signs in, consent decides which of that user's accounts you connect to. You can send both.
75: select_account is not supported
76: prompt=select_account is not supported. Use prompt=consent to let the user choose which Brex account the token represents.
77: Implementing your own client
78: If you need to implement your own client, we recommend starting with the developer guides from Okta and reading below for more details. The scopes for your client will be provided to you.
79: Authorization Code Grant
80: 1. Request authorization code
81: This is a redirection-based flow, which means that the application must be capable of interacting with the user-agent (i.e. the Brex client’s web browser) and receiving API authorization codes that are routed through the user-agent.
82: https://accounts-api.brex.com/oauth2/default/v1/authorize?client_id=<CLIENT_ID>&response_type=code&redirect_uri=<REDIRECT_URI>&scope=<SCOPES>&state=<STATE>
83: Parameters:
84: client_id=<CLIENT_ID>: The client id provided by Brex.
85: response_type=code: Specifies that your application is requesting an authorization code grant.
86: redirect_uri=<REDIRECT_URI>: Where the service redirects the user-agent after an authorization code is granted. Must match exactly one of the addresses that was provided to Brex when the credentials were set up.
87: scope=<SCOPES>: Scopes requested, separated by whitespaces.
88: state=<STATE>: A required parameter that must be longer than 8 characters. For more details about state parameter, please check https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc6749#section-10.12.
89: OAuth PKCE flow: Also supported, but not required.
90: 2. The Brex client authorizes the application
91: When the browser link is opened, the Brex client will be prompted to sign in to authenticate their identity. They will then be prompted to authorize or deny your application's access to their account. They may accept 0 to all of the requested scopes which your application will then have access to. If they cancel consent, you will not have any scopes granted.
92: Because the client can decline individual scopes, a successful authorization does not mean the token will contain the scopes that were requested. Compare the scope value on the redirect URL against what you requested, and gracefully handle the affected features from the response instead of assuming the full set of scopes from the request. A scope you requested and did not receive will produce an HTTP 403 on every API call that needs the scope.
93: A granted scope is also not the same as a working one — the account must have the underlying product, and the user must hold the required role. See a granted scope is not a guarantee of access.
94: If the Brex client authorizes the request, we'll redirect the user-agent to your application's redirect URI, along with an authorization code. The redirect will look like this:
95: <REDIRECT_URI>?code=<AUTHORIZATION_CODE>&scope=<SCOPES>&state=<STATE>
96: Parameters:
97: code=<AUTHORIZATION_CODE>: The authorization code that can be used to request an access token.
98: scope=<SCOPES>: Scopes that were granted by the Brex client and can be a subset of what was requested.
99: state=<STATE>: For security reasons, you should always confirm that the returned state matches the value you provided in the request.
100: 3. Request an access token
101: To request an access token from the API, pass the authorization code along with authentication details to the API token endpoint. Here is an cURL example request:
102: curl '{staging or production base auth URL}/v1/token' \
103: --header 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' \
104: --data-urlencode 'grant_type=authorization_code' \
105: --data-urlencode 'code={AUTHORIZATION_CODE}' \
106: --data-urlencode 'redirect_uri={REDIRECT_URI}' \
107: --data-urlencode 'client_id={CLIENT_ID}' \
108: --data-urlencode 'client_secret={CLIENT_SECRET}'
109: Response body:
110: access_token: "<ACCESS_TOKEN>"
111: refresh_token: "<REFRESH_TOKEN>"
112: token_type: "bearer"
113: The access token returned expires in 3600 seconds (1 hour) and you will need to get a new one (see step 5) every time after it expires. Getting a new access token does not require the user to re-authorize the request.
114: 4. Using an access token
115: Add your <ACCESS_TOKEN> as a bearer token into the request header of any API calls you are making on behalf of the customer.
116: Request header:
117: Authorization: Bearer <ACCESS_TOKEN>
118: 5. Getting a new access token and refresh token
119: To obtain a new access token, pass in the <REFRESH_TOKEN> previously obtained by the token endpoint, and set grant_type=refresh_token.
120: The response will contain a new <ACCESS_TOKEN> as well as a new REFRESH_TOKEN. Refresh tokens rotate, so store the new one and discard the old; the refresh token you just used will not work a second time.
121: A refresh carries forward the grant you already have. The new access token represents the same account and the same scopes as the original authorization; refreshing never broadens scopes and never changes which account the token represents. To change either, send the user through the authorization flow again.
122: Refresh tokens expire every 90 days so they should be exchanged for a new one before then. Failure to do so will require the user to re-authenticate.
123: Client Credentials Grant
124: 1. Request client credentials
125: Request an access token using grant_type=client_credentials and your Brex provided credentials from the token endpoint.
126: Scopes are defined as a space delimited list such as: cards cards.readonly. Make sure to request the relevant scopes in the access token request to use the appropriate APIs.
127: An example cURL request:
128: curl '{staging or production base auth URL}/v1/token' \
129: --header 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' \
130: --data-urlencode 'grant_type=client_credentials' \
131: --data-urlencode 'client_id={CLIENT_ID}' \
132: --data-urlencode 'client_secret={CLIENT_SECRET}' \
133: --data-urlencode 'scope={SCOPES}'
134: An example response body:
135: {
136: "access_token": "<ACCESS_TOKEN>",
137: "expires_in": 3600,
138: "scope": "<SCOPES>",
139: "token_type": "Bearer"
140: }
141: 2. Using an access token
142: Add your <ACCESS_TOKEN> as a bearer token into the request header of any API calls you are making on behalf of the customer.
143: Request header:
144: Authorization: Bearer <ACCESS_TOKEN>
145: The access token returned expires in 3600 seconds (1 hour). If you don't prefer to persistently store and rotate tokens, you can simply request a new token when it expires.
146: Revoking refresh tokens
147: Refresh tokens expire every 90 days. However, for general best security practices, or in the event of a compromise, you may want to revoke your refresh token. In order to do so, hit the refresh token revocation endpoint:
148: POST "{staging or production base URL}/v1/revoke"
149: // Request Body
150: {
151: "token": "<refresh-token-to-revoke>",
152: "client_id": "OAuth2 client id used to get the refresh token",
153: "client_secret": "OAuth2 client secret used to get the refresh token"
154: }
155: Redirect URIs
156: OAuth 2.0 depends on Redirect URIs for the Authorization Code Grant. Partners must supply one or more redirect URIs that Brex will use to post the authorization code. (See Authentication implementation > Authorization Code Grant > 2. The Brex client authorizes the application)
157: Was this helpful?

159: Next pageUser roles and permissions

21: This changelog tracks changes to the Brex API and is updated periodically. Updates to the API are on a rolling basis and not on any defined schedule.
22: November 2026
23: Team API: Added List roles (GET /v2/roles) and the roles and roles.readonly OAuth scopes. The endpoint lists the custom roles defined for the account.
24: Team API: Added display_name to custom field objects returned when load_custom_fields is set.
25: Team API: Added role_name to Invite user. Set it to the role's dashboard name, including a custom role's display_name from List roles. When it is omitted, the user is invited as an employee and receives physical and virtual card access by default.
26: Team API: Added role_name to Update user. It replaces the user's current role. Their card access is unchanged.
27: Team API: Added role_name to user objects returned by the user endpoints. It is the user's role as shown in the Brex dashboard.
28: Accounting API: added the new REIMBURSEMENT_PURCHASE_DATE_TOO_OLD enum value to the error_code response property
29: Accounting API (Alpha): Published amortization templates, VAT tax codes and tax groups, and Update accounting records. These endpoints are in alpha.
30: October 2026
31: Expenses API: Added the load_expense_addenda query parameter to the expense endpoints and an addenda array on expense objects, with structured purchase data such as lodging, trip leg, train, and attendee details. Clarified that amounts are keyed by lowercase currency code and that clients should skip addenda with an unrecognized type.
32: Expenses API: Added HELD to ExpensePaymentStatus for bill payments on hold until the vendor's new payment method is approved. Added the optional display_name field to custom field objects.
33: Payments API: Added imad and omad to transfer objects returned by List transfers, Get transfer, and Create transfer. They are populated for domestic and international wires when available.
34: September 2026
35: Team API: Added Create user (POST /v2/users/create) to create an inactive employee without sending an invitation.
36: Team API: Added update and delete endpoints for departments, locations, and titles.
37: Team API: Added List cost centers and Get cost center, including the cost_centers and cost_centers.readonly OAuth scopes.
38: Team API: Expanded the statuses accepted by Update user to support archiving and restoring inactive users and deleting invited or inactive users.
39: Team API: Added filter query parameters to List users: name, email[], status[], manager_id[], department_id[], location_id[], title_id[], cost_center_id[], legal_entity_id[], and custom_field[]. The legacy singular email and remote_display_id parameters cannot be combined with these filters.
40: Team API: Added cost_center_id and legal_entity_id to user objects returned by the List users, Get current user, and Get user endpoints, and as optional fields on Invite user and Update user.
41: Team API: Added the load_custom_fields query parameter to List users, Get current user, and Get user, along with a custom_fields array on the user object. This replaces the expand[] query parameter on List users.
42: Team API: Removed the Get limit for the user endpoint (GET /v2/users/{id}/limit).
43: Team API: Removed the deprecated POST /v2/users/{id}/limit endpoint (setUserLimit); it is no longer supported.
44: August 2026
45: Travel API: Removed the deprecated INVITED value from the Trip.Status enum; this status is no longer used.
46: Travel API: Added policy to booking objects, exposing whether a booking was out of policy and which travel policy rules it violated. This mirrors the policy information available in the booking export.
47: Expenses API: Added cost_center_id and the expandable cost_center object to expense objects, and cost_center as an expand option on the expenses endpoints.
48: Transactions API: Documented that List primary card transactions may reflect a small lag, and recommended using a lookback window of at least one day when syncing transactions so delayed transactions are not missed.
49: July 2026
50: Travel API: Added the load_custom_fields query parameter to the list trips, get trip, list bookings, and get booking endpoints, along with a custom_fields array on trip and booking objects.
51: Transactions API: Documented the recommended use of an overlapping lookback window on posted_at_start when polling the card and cash transaction endpoints, so that transactions are not missed when a request fails or a transaction posts late.
52: June 2026
53: Expenses API: Added compliance_status[] and derived_compliance_status[] filters to the List expenses endpoints, allowing expenses that are missing required documentation to be listed.
54: April 2026
55: MCP Server (Beta): Launched the Brex MCP server. Connect AI assistants like Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, and Codex to your Brex account. Query expenses, look up users, check card statuses, and more through natural language. Supports OAuth and API key authentication.
56: Team API: Added created_at and partner to the card object. card_name is now nullable and is no longer a required property.
57: Expenses API: Added card_transaction_reference_id to expense objects, providing a reference identifier for the underlying card transaction.
58: Expenses API: Added booking_id field to expense objects, providing the booking ID for trip expenses.
59: Expenses API: Added spending_entity and policy as expand options on the List Expenses endpoints.
60: Onboarding API: Updated accepted EIN document types to include CP-575 fax sheet.
61: March 2026
62: Onboarding API: Added new endpoint POST /v1/referrals/{id}/process_ein_document for processing delayed EIN documents after upload.
63: Fields API: Added TRAVEL field type to field definitions.
64: Webhooks API: Added ACCOUNTING_RECORD_READY_FOR_EXPORT webhook event with schema and documentation.
65: Transactions API: Added card_transaction_operation_reference_id field to card transaction objects.
66: Team API: Updated secure endpoint URLs to new api.brex.com hostnames.
67: February 2026
68: Expenses API: Reduced maximum limit parameter from 1000 to 100 for the List Expenses endpoints.
69: Updated the API documentation look and feel.
70: January 2026
71: Accounting API (GA): The core Accounting API is generally available. It covers accounting integrations and accounting records: create, get, list, disconnect, and reactivate an integration, and query, get, and report export results for accounting records.
72: Added support for new API hostnames (api.brex.com); the former hostnames will continue to work for the forseeable future.
73: December 2025
74: Expenses API: Added dashboard_url field to expense objects, providing a direct link to view expenses in the Brex dashboard.
75: November 2025
76: Accounting API (Alpha): Published the Accounting API reference so ERP partners or customers can discover and integrate with accounting data endpoints.
77: Fields API (Beta): Field definition now exposes an optional integration_id and a new ERP field type. This allows API caller to associate an ERP field with specific integration.
78: Webhooks API: Expanded WebhookEventType to include ACCOUNTING_RECORD_READY_FOR_EXPORT event type (Alpha).
79: May 2025
80: Cards API: Updated spend controls documentation with improved nullable property definitions.
81: Fields API (alpha): Added official Fields API documentation with comprehensive endpoint specifications, including field creation, updates, and retrieval operations.
82: Expenses API: Deprecated Card Expenses API endpoints in favor of consolidated Expenses API endpoints.
83: April 2025
84: Expenses API: Added documentation for new payment_posted_at_start and payment_posted_at_end filters in the List expenses endpoints, allowing filtering expenses by when payments were posted.
85: March 2025
86: Expenses API: Updated documentation with latest field additions, including improved custom fields documentation.
87: Expenses API: Published new endpoints and added spending_entity documentation to provide better visibility into expense attribution.
88: January 2025
89: Budgets API: Updated spend limit creation to support legal_entity_id and department_id parameters, allowing expenses to be attributed to specific entities and departments.
90: Team API: Added new endpoint to get a legal entity by ID (GET /v2/legal_entities/{id}).
91: Repository: Updated CODEOWNERS file to reflect team-specific ownership of different API sections.
92: December 2024
93: Team API: The Get card number endpoint response object now includes the cardholder name (holder_name).
94: Expenses API: The List expenses endpoint request now allows for filtering on the updated_at timestamp of expenses.
95: October 2024
96: Payments API: New endpoints introduced to create incoming transfers, list bank connections, manage transfers, and manage vendor information.
97: Budgets API: Introduced new spend limit and budgets concepts as a new set of API endpoints (v2). The old Spend Limits (v1) API is considered deprecated.
98: September 2024
99: Team API: The Get card endpoint response object now returns a (has_been_transferred) boolean for a given card.
100: Team API: The Create card endpoint response object now accepts an expense policy ID (policy_id) boolean for a given card.
101: Expenses API: The Expense object now returns an optional address (has_been_transferred), a payment posted date and a trip ID if relevant to the expense.
102: July 2024
103: Webhooks: Updated IP whitelist.
104: February 2022
105: Transactions API: The List cash accounts endpoint response object now includes a primary boolean field indicating whether the cash account is the primary cash account for the Brex account. Every Brex user must have one primary cash account.
106: All APIs: Added a new header for tracing with a generic name X-Brex-Trace-Id. Although the previous header X-Datadog-Trace-Id is still in use as of now, we recommend to start using X-Brex-Trace-Id as it is vendor-agnostic and will unlikely change overtime.
107: Payments API: Added cancellation_reason into the Transfer response.
108: January 2022
109: Webhooks API: Added beta support for webhooks. View the webhooks guide for how to get started and the webhooks API reference for supported events and how to use them.
110: Team API: Added a monthly_available object to the responses for both the GET and SET methods for user limits
111: December 2021
112: Payments API: Added the ability to do book transfers between Brex Cash accounts. See counterparty -> type -> BOOK_TRANSFER in the request body for the Create Transfer endpoint
113: November 2021
114: Transactions API: Added endpoints to read cash transactions and read primary card transactions
115: October 2021
116: Payments API: Added the ability to filter vendors by name (via encoded query param) for the lists vendors endpoint
117: Was this helpful?
118: Copyright © Brex LLC 2019–2026. All rights reserved.
119: Ask AI

14: Plaid has one environment for development (Sandbox) and one for live use (Production). Trial plan and Limited Production are two ways to access Production for free, on a limited basis, before applying for full paid access. Use the table below to find the right one for your stage; details on each follow.

49: Sandbox
50: The Sandbox is a free environment for application development and testing with mock data. It supports all Plaid functionality, including the Plaid API and Plaid Link. The Sandbox provides a variety of test accounts and institutions to test against, and developers can create an unlimited number of test Items.
51: The Sandbox is designed for development purposes and does not interact with any real data, which is ideal for developers who are experimenting with Plaid or still working out the bugs in their application.
52: Production
53: Use the Production environment to deploy an application with Plaid's products or to test with live data. This environment provides access to real data.
54: Approval for the Production environment takes a couple of business days, and you'll need to provide more information about your company and how you plan to use the Plaid API. The Plaid Dashboard walks you through the process of requesting Production access.
55: Trial plan
56: For developers in the US and Canada who sign up on or after April 15, 2026, Plaid offers a Trial plan — a free way to use Plaid with real production data before applying for full Production access. Trial plans are auto-approved for most developers and support up to 10 Production Items. Eight core products are included: Auth, Transactions (including Transactions Refresh), Balance, Identity, Assets, Liabilities, Investments (including Investments Refresh), and Statements. Trial plan developers also have access to OAuth institutions without needing to complete the full Production registration process.
57: To start a Trial plan, create a Dashboard account and verify your email address, then complete the Trial plan application form.
58: If you need more than 10 Items, or need products not included in the Trial bundle, you will need to apply for full Production access.
59: Limited Production
60: Note: As of April 15, 2026, new Limited Production signups are no longer available for developers in the US and Canada. If you are a new US/CA developer, see "Trial plan" above. Existing Limited Production customers retain access.
61: Limited Production is a special mode of the Production environment that is available for some Plaid products and can be used to try the Plaid API with real data before obtaining full Production access. In Limited Production, you have access to Plaid's Production server and can make a limited number of free API calls, but your API usage is capped and some functionality is unavailable. Unlike Sandbox, Limited Production is not a separate environment from Production. For more details on Limited Production, see Testing with Real Data in Limited Production.

21: Hi! I'm Bill! You can ask me all about the Plaid API. Try asking questions like:Pssst -- I also moonlight as your IDE's research librarian! Plug me in via the Plaid MCP Server.
22: Note: Bill isn't perfect. He's just a robot platypus that reads our docs for fun. You should treat his answers with the same healthy skepticism you might treat any other answer on the internet. This chat may be logged for quality and training purposes. Please don't send Bill any PII -- he's scared of intimacy. All chats with Bill are subject to Plaid's Privacy Policy.
23: Dashboard MCP server
24: Connect an LLM application to Plaid Dashboard tools
25: Plaid offers two Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers:
26: The Dashboard MCP server is a remote MCP server hosted by Plaid. It provides Production diagnostics and analytics tools, including tools for debugging Items, reviewing Link conversion data, and checking usage metrics.
27: The Plaid AI coding toolkit includes a local MCP server for development. It runs as a subprocess of an MCP client, such as Claude, Cursor, Codex, VS Code, or Zed, and provides tools for mock data generation, documentation search, Sandbox tokens, and webhook simulation.
28: This article covers the Dashboard MCP server. You can connect to it from an MCP client, or you can use it in a model provider's API as a remote MCP server.
29: The Dashboard MCP server is under active development. Breaking changes may occur, and Plaid currently provides limited support.
30: Connection options
31: Requirements
32: The Dashboard MCP server works with Production data only. Your team must be approved for Production access with at least one Plaid product to use the MCP server.
33: MCP client setup
34: Use this option for an MCP client or hosted assistant, such as Claude.ai, ChatGPT, or another client that supports remote MCP server URLs.
35: In your client's MCP settings, add the Dashboard MCP server URL:
36: Dashboard MCP server URL
37: https://api.dashboard.plaid.com/mcp/
38: If your client asks for the transport or protocol, choose Streamable HTTP.
39: For Claude.ai setup, see Claude's custom connector documentation.
40: API integration with remote MCP
41: Use this option when your application calls a model provider API and lets the model call Dashboard MCP tools during that request. This is an API integration with a remote MCP server. OpenAI exposes remote MCP servers as mcp tools in the Responses API. Anthropic calls this feature the MCP connector in the Messages API.
42: For this flow, your backend creates or refreshes a Plaid OAuth token and passes it to the model provider SDK with the Dashboard MCP server URL. The field name depends on the provider. OpenAI uses authorization; Anthropic uses authorization_token.
43: Your model provider account must have access to remote MCP servers or hosted tools.
44: Creating an OAuth token
45: To connect to the Dashboard MCP server, first create an OAuth token with the mcp:dashboard scope and the client_credentials grant type by calling /oauth/token.
46: Creating an access token
47: curl -X POST https://production.plaid.com/oauth/token \
48: -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
49: -d '{
50: "client_id": "${PLAID_CLIENT_ID}",
51: "client_secret": "YOUR_PRODUCTION_SECRET",
52: "grant_type": "client_credentials",
53: "scope": "mcp:dashboard"
54: }'
55: The response includes an access_token for Dashboard MCP requests and a refresh_token for requesting a new access token.
56: Passing the MCP server to a model API
57: The Dashboard MCP server is available at https://api.dashboard.plaid.com/mcp/ and uses the Streamable HTTP protocol. When you communicate with the MCP server directly, pass the access_token from the authorization step in an Authorization: Bearer <access_token> header.
58: The connection method depends on the LLM client library. Most provider SDKs expose remote MCP servers as tools that the model can call. See your model provider's documentation, such as OpenAI or Anthropic. Use a current version of your model provider's client library.
59: The following examples show how to access Link analytics through the Dashboard MCP server using the OpenAI or Anthropic Python client libraries.
60: These examples use the following environment variables: PLAID_CLIENT_ID, PLAID_PRODUCTION_SECRET, and either OPENAI_API_KEY or ANTHROPIC_API_KEY.
61: Select group for content switcher
62: OpenAIAnthropic
63: OpenAI Python example
64: import json
65: import os
66: import plaid
67: from openai import OpenAI
68: from plaid.api import plaid_api
69: from plaid.api_client import ApiClient
70: from plaid.model.o_auth_grant_type import OAuthGrantType
71: from plaid.model.o_auth_token_request import OAuthTokenRequest
72: DASHBOARD_MCP_SERVER_URL = "https://api.dashboard.plaid.com/mcp/"
73: def get_plaid_client():
74: configuration = plaid.Configuration(
75: host=plaid.Environment.Production,
76: api_key={
77: "clientId": os.environ["PLAID_CLIENT_ID"],
78: "secret": os.environ["PLAID_PRODUCTION_SECRET"],
79: },
80: )
81: api_client = ApiClient(configuration)
82: return plaid_api.PlaidApi(api_client)
83: def request_or_refresh_access_token():
84: # This example creates a new access token each run.
85: plaid_client = get_plaid_client()
86: oauth_token_request = OAuthTokenRequest(
87: grant_type=OAuthGrantType("client_credentials"),
88: scope="mcp:dashboard",
89: )
90: response = plaid_client.oauth_token(oauth_token_request)
91: return response.access_token
92: def main() -> None:
93: """Retrieve Link analytics through the Dashboard MCP server."""
94: client = OpenAI(api_key=os.environ["OPENAI_API_KEY"])
95: dashboard_token = request_or_refresh_access_token()
96: response = client.responses.create(
97: model="gpt-5.5",
98: tools=[
99: {
100: "type": "mcp",
101: "server_label": "plaid",
102: "server_url": DASHBOARD_MCP_SERVER_URL,
103: "require_approval": "never",
104: "authorization": dashboard_token,
105: }
106: ],
107: input=(
108: "Use the Dashboard MCP server to get Link analytics from "
109: "2025-05-01 through 2025-05-08. Return Link opens, "
110: "institution selections, and handoffs."
111: ),
112: )
113: for item in response.output:
114: if item.type == "mcp_list_tools":
115: print("\n=== MCP Tools ===")
116: for tool in item.tools:
117: print(f" - {tool['name']}")
118: elif item.type == "mcp_call":
119: print("\n=== MCP Call ===")
120: print(f"Tool: {item.name}")
121: try:
122: # The arguments field is a JSON string. Parse it for readability.
123: args = json.loads(item.arguments)
124: except (TypeError, json.JSONDecodeError):
125: args = item.arguments
126: print("Arguments:")
127: print(json.dumps(args, indent=2))
128: elif item.type == "message":
129: print("\n=== Assistant Message ===")
130: # The content field is a list of ResponseOutputText objects.
131: texts = []
132: for part in item.content:
133: # Depending on SDK version, `text` may be an attribute or dict key.
134: text = getattr(part, "text", None) or (
135: part.get("text") if isinstance(part, dict) else None
136: )
137: if text:
138: texts.append(text)
139: print("\n".join(texts))
140: else:
141: print(f"\n=== Unhandled output type: {item.type} ===")
142: print(item)
143: if __name__ == "__main__":
144: main()
145: Sample output
146: === MCP Tools ===
147: - plaid_debug_item
148: - plaid_get_link_analytics
149: - plaid_get_tools_introduction
150: - plaid_get_usages
151: - plaid_list_teams
152: === MCP Call ===
153: Tool: plaid_list_teams
154: Arguments:
155: {}
156: === MCP Call ===
157: Tool: plaid_get_link_analytics
158: Arguments:
159: {
160: "from_date": "2025-05-01",
161: "team_id": "<team_id>",
162: "to_date": "2025-05-08"
163: }
164: === Assistant Message ===
165: From 2025-05-01 through 2025-05-08:
166: - Link opens: 58
167: - Institution selections: 29
168: - Handoffs: 18
169: Expired tokens
170: Access tokens for the MCP server expire after 15 minutes. If the access token expires, MCP requests fail with a 401 status code or a provider-specific authentication error. Create a new token or call /oauth/token with the refresh_token.
171: Refreshing an access token
172: curl -X POST https://production.plaid.com/oauth/token \
173: -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
174: -d '{
175: "client_id": "${PLAID_CLIENT_ID}",
176: "client_secret": "YOUR_PRODUCTION_SECRET",
177: "refresh_token": "YOUR_REFRESH_TOKEN",
178: "grant_type": "refresh_token"
179: }'
180: Dashboard MCP tools

1: # Binance MCP 2:

3: 4:            5: 6:

7:

8: A TypeScript MCP server for Binance market data, account insights, and Convert workflows. 9:

10:

11: 12: 13: 14:

15: ## What This Server Does 16: `binance-mcp` exposes a focused set of MCP tools for working with Binance data from Claude Desktop or any MCP-compatible client. 17: It covers: 18: - Live spot prices 19: - Best bid/ask quotes 20: - Spot account balances 21: - Funding wallet balances 22: - Combined account and portfolio views 23: - Binance Convert quote and order workflows 24: - Convert trade history 25: ## Tools 26: | Tool | Purpose | Auth | 27: | --- | --- | --- | 28: | `get_last_prices` | Fetch latest last-traded prices for one or more spot symbols | No | 29: | `get_book_ticker` | Fetch current best bid and ask for one or more spot symbols | No | 30: | `get_spot_account` | Return spot account balances and account flags | Yes | 31: | `get_funding_wallet` | Return funding wallet balances | Yes | 32: | `get_account_overview` | Merge spot and funding balances into one view | Yes | 33: | `get_portfolio_snapshot` | Build a live valuation snapshot across balances and prices | Yes | 34: | `get_convert_quote` | Request a Binance Convert quote without executing it | Yes | 35: | `accept_convert_quote` | Execute a live Convert quote | Yes | 36: | `get_convert_order_status` | Check the status of a Convert order | Yes | 37: | `get_convert_trade_history` | Fetch Convert trade history for a time window | Yes | 38: ## Why This MCP Is Useful 39: - Keeps Binance workflows inside your AI assistant instead of switching between apps. 40: - Separates safe quote retrieval from live trade execution. 41: - Uses short-lived market-data caching and websocket updates for fast price lookups. 42: - Returns structured JSON so Claude can reason over balances, prices, and conversions cleanly. 43: ## Quick Start 44: ### 1. Install dependencies 45: ```bash 46: npm install 47: ``` 48: ### 2. Build the server 49: ```bash 50: npm run build 51: ``` 52: ### 3. Run locally 53: ```bash 54: npm start 55: ``` 56: The server communicates over `stdio`, which is the standard transport used by Claude Desktop. 57: ## Full Documentation 58: If you want the deeper implementation notes, endpoint details, and design rationale, see [DOCUMENTATION.md](DOCUMENTATION.md). 59: ## Claude Desktop Setup 60: Use the compiled server entry point in your claude_desktop_config.json file. 61: ### Example configuration 62: ```json 63: { 64: "mcpServers": { 65: "binance-mcp": { 66: "command": "node", 67: "args": ["C:/Binance-mcp/build/index.js"], 68: "env": { 69: "BINANCE_API_KEY": "your_api_key", 70: "BINANCE_API_SECRET": "your_api_secret" 71: } 72: } 73: } 74: } 75: ``` 76: ### Notes 77: - Public market tools work without credentials. 78: - Account and Convert tools require `BINANCE_API_KEY` and `BINANCE_API_SECRET`. 79: - If you want to customize Binance endpoints, you can override the environment variables listed below. 80: ## Environment Variables 81: | Variable | Default | Purpose | 82: | --- | --- | --- | 83: | `BINANCE_API_KEY` | none | Binance API key for signed endpoints | 84: | `BINANCE_API_SECRET` | none | Binance API secret for request signing | 85: | `BINANCE_BASE_URL` | `https://api.binance.com` | Base URL for signed REST requests | 86: | `BINANCE_PUBLIC_BASE_URL` | `https://data-api.binance.vision` | Base URL for public market-data requests | 87: | `BINANCE_STREAM_BASE_URL` | `wss://stream.binance.com:9443/stream` | Binance websocket stream endpoint | 88: | `BINANCE_TIMEOUT_MS` | `8000` | Request timeout in milliseconds | 89: | `BINANCE_RECV_WINDOW_MS` | `5000` | Binance signed request recvWindow | 90: | `BINANCE_MAX_RETRIES` | `1` | Retry attempts for safe requests | 91: | `BINANCE_PRICE_CACHE_TTL_MS` | `1500` | Freshness window for market-data cache | 92: | `BINANCE_STREAM_ENABLED` | `true` | Enables websocket price streaming | 93: ## Example Usage 94: ### Price lookup 95: ```text 96: Get the latest price for BTCUSDT and ETHUSDT. 97: ``` 98: ### Portfolio snapshot 99: ```text 100: Show my portfolio snapshot in USDT. 101: ``` 102: ### Convert flow 103: ```text 104: Create a Convert quote from BTC to USDT for 0.01 BTC, then show the quote details. 105: ``` 106: ## Build and Implementation Details 107: This project is implemented in TypeScript and uses the official MCP SDK. 108: - `src/index.ts` registers MCP tools and formats responses. 109: - `src/binance.ts` handles Binance REST calls, HMAC signing, websocket market data, retries, and portfolio math. 110: - `build/index.js` is the compiled entry point used by Claude Desktop. 111: ## Safety 112: - `accept_convert_quote` performs a live conversion. 113: - Signed endpoints are unavailable until API credentials are present. 114: - Convert quotes should always be reviewed before execution. 115: - Binance rate limits still apply, so avoid unnecessary polling. 116: ## License 117: Released under the MIT License. See [LICENSE](LICENSE).
